articles.title: Our Experiences are Interconnected, Regardless of Citizenship - The Forge
articles.content: The politics of divide and conquer are as present as ever, and so how do we gather all that has happened already and take that technology that we have developed — that comes from our creativity, that comes from our hearts, that comes from our spiritual spaces, that comes from our learnings of being in community, and being on these battlefields together — and sharpen those tools? Miski Noor: Nana, I want to start with the fact that your organizing experience is both deep and wide. And so, I’d like to just start with grounding us there. Please tell us what brings you to this work. Nana Gyamfi: I come to this work because it’s part of the work of Black liberation, which is really important to me. It’s been my life’s work in different ways and forms, whether it has been as an organizer coming up in the ‘80s and ‘90s — because I’m old as dirt and twice as funky — or whether it’s been as a movement attorney that has represented folks who are organizers, who have engaged in protest, who’ve been targeted by the state in one way or another. Whether it’s been as a professor in the Pan-African Studies Department, where I was able to work with young folks who were organizing and trying to get young folks into organizing, or operating now as the Executive Director of BAJI (Black Alliance for Just Immigration). It’s all been about Black liberation. How do we build the power that we need in order to change the conditions of our people and have us be more free? MN: Thank you for that. To continue with what you named about building power, please bring us into the current moment: with the unrelenting attacks on immigrants by this current administration in the White House, how is BAJI responding in this moment, and what does your work look like? I am particularly interested in the Black migrant ecosystem that y’all have been working inside of. NG: I think what we’ve been really trying to do is see how we engage in the work that we engage in, which, yes, is organizing work. There’s a civic engagement piece which we just sort of bind up in a discussion of our power building team. There is legal and policy advocacy work, there is work around culture shift and narrative building. There’s work around research and reports. So that’s how we’re connecting all of the dots, giving ourselves and our communities more spaces, more ways to be able to jump into this work, helping them to understand that some of this work they’re doing already. It may not be under the title of an organization but, you know, you’re already in the process of fighting for Black liberation in the space that you’re in. And it’s really about how do we bring all of that together so that we’re aligned, so that we’re moving in a way together that allows us to actually do so in a powerful way, which is what the Black migrant ecosystem is about. It’s not a coalition. It’s really a mass organizing space where Black individuals, regardless of immigrant status or citizenship, are able to come and work together. You don’t have to be part of an organization, you know. You don’t have to be part of a 501(c)3. You might be part of a cadre or collective, you may not be. It might be just you and there’s work that you’re doing in your community: you’re concerned about what’s happening with your community, and you want to jump in and see what you can do. So it’s a place to get information about what is happening. It’s a place to share information about what is happening in your neighborhood, what’s happening in, you know, your local community or statewide community, or happening with your group of folks that you’re engaging with in terms of Black folks, and particularly Black immigrants. It’s a space where people can get some training or technical skills that people are looking for. It’s a space where people can talk about some of the things that they’re afraid of, some of the things that they’re concerned about in a safe space. Because it’s a space that’s open to all Black people, where we really want to lift up the best of queer feminist abolitionist values, centering the people who are the most marginalized, the people who are the most impacted by all of these oppressive systems. So we have a consistent crew of people that show up and show out, you know, in terms of getting and sharing information and really being willing to dig in. And we’re excited about moving that to being more in-person as well as continuing the virtual work that we’re doing, and seeing how we can have this space also be more intergenerational. How do we use the information and the technology that people have been using and see how we can apply it in this time? We have people who have been fighting in the Civil Rights movement, the Black Power movement, the war on drugs (which was really the war on Black people), the Movement for Black Lives; there’s so many lessons just there, and those aren’t the only movements that Black people have been a part of, that Black people have led, including Black immigrants. So let’s say we got folks still kicking and doing the darn thing in their 80s, right? All the way to these young folks that we see walking out of schools. How do we gather all that has happened already and take that technology that we have developed — that comes from our creativity, that comes from our hearts, that comes from our spiritual spaces, that comes from our learnings of being in community, and being on these battlefields together — and sharpen those tools? To get clarity, learn lessons, and repent for the past, in terms of transgressions, and work with each other, heal some wounds, so that we can be even more powerful as we face a more snarling, snapping foe than some of us have in a long time. MN: Thank you so much for sharing with me the expansiveness of the network y’all are building and the connections it is making, Nana. I’m going to bring us back out wider to one of the goals of your work: to cultivate global Black solidarity. And so, for people who may be unfamiliar with transnational solidarity work, what does that mean? What does your international work look like in particular? NG: This, to me, is like the crux of really our power, this transnational work. And I think that history bears that out, right? Where we have gotten action is when it has been transnational. Some cases we know, and in some cases that we’ve read and learned about, have to do with people that were in the Black Liberation Army. People that depended on some transnational solidarity. That’s why Mama Assata was still in Cuba. Our folks remember, even within the Black Panther Party — not even going to the military side of it — even with the Black Panther Party, they went to Algeria. You had people that went to Tanzania. You had people that went to Ghana, right? What do we learn from Black queer folks in Ghana, in Uganda, in Nigeria, about what it means to be in situations where your existence is criminalized and you don’t want to leave? So we’ve had that solidarity that is on the “We Got Us” level. That has enabled us to do what we needed to do in terms of our liberation movements. When we decided that we were concerned about Black folks in South Africa, and we were going to make sure that that apartheid regime ended, that was a transnational effort. Haiti is even in people’s brains, because of the transnational effort of Black people. If it wasn’t for that, nobody would be talking about Haiti. And to the degree that we hear people now talking about Sudan, talking about the Congo, etc, it’s been because of a transnational effort. So there’s a number of things that we look at as we’re looking at how we engage transnationally. One piece of it is the work that we are doing as part of the Cross movement table over at M4BL, being a lead at that table and really looking at how liberation movements or movements for power were successful and what are the lessons we can learn from that. What are the lessons that we can learn from our cousins and siblings in these other countries who actually have been in positions of power, who are the left — I’m gonna use that language — who are progressive, who are looking towards liberation. And what are the lessons we learned? What works, what doesn’t work? What technologies they may have had, what tools, what things they didn’t see coming? How do we make sure that we see that coming? What are the things there? Part of it is about the political education piece, so that our folks are not saying things like, “this is not our fight”, but also, that people are understanding what is the fight, why it is they’re fighting, and what are some of the tools with regard to that fight. Part of it is showing up in civil society on the international level, and being part of coalitions or conversations that are regular with our folks that are on the continent, with our folks that are in the Caribbean, with Black folks that are in South America, and in Central America, and in Europe, and in Canada. Really engaging in conversations, comparing and contrasting, and seeing how we can be in collaboration with one another on some of these issues that we want to deal with, in our home countries, in each other’s countries, but also just on a global level. And then we’re trying to engage in the global institutional spaces. So, you know, engaging with the UN Permanent Forum for People of African descent. When UNPOL, which is the UN agency that looks at police and policing, came to the U.S. to do a report, we were engaged both in Los Angeles and in New York in terms of testifying and organizing events. We also organized ourselves with respect to the Inter-American Human Rights Council, and we’ve done reports with them. That’s mainly been about Mexico, Central America, South America, and the Caribbean to some degree, these different international institutional spaces that we’ve also been in. So, we’ve been trying to engage in these conversations. MN: So my next question kind of continues on the same thread. Can you talk to me about how Black people, regardless of immigration status or citizenship, are impacted by anti-Blackness? What are the connections between the prison industrial complex and immigration detention practices, and what are the consequences for Black communities if we do not understand how the two work together? NG: So, it’s a serious situation because what we see happening right now is this expansion of the police state. It’s partially because there hasn’t been a good understanding of how anti-Blackness and criminalization are connected, and how that then becomes something that impacts people, even when they’re not Black. When we look at the criminalization of Blackness that is resulting from the enslavement of Black people in this country, and obviously outside of this country, it’s rooted in imperialism, colonialism, and enslavement — chattel slavery — that’s what it’s rooted in. When you’re talking about those three things, you’re automatically talking about militarism, right? Because that’s how you engage in imperialism and colonialism. You’re automatically talking about that sort of domestic form of militarism, which is policing. So it starts on that criminalization side and that side is a side that doesn’t come out of any sense of justice. That doesn’t come out of any sense of righting the wrong. That only comes out of a sense of punishment and control, particularly of Black people. And we say “racial capitalism,” but as Ruthie Gilmore has pointed out, there’s no such thing as any other kind of capitalism. Automatically you’re saying racial. Automatically you’re saying gender. Automatically you’re saying poverty. You’re already saying these things, but just using that term for now, in terms of racial capitalism, it is anti-Blackness that comes with a big side of profit, right? And so when we look at slavery by another name, we see that literally the law was manipulated through the use of white power and white control to create scenarios in which Black people could just be rounded up and imprisoned for the purposes of money. Whether that was debt collection, or whether that was because they were leased out to private entities, or because they were substituted, like the California firefighters , for the cost of hiring people that you actually gotta pay a wage and health insurance and pensions to. That creates this frenzied situation, which just extends the frenzied situation of the transatlantic kidnapping and enslavement of people. And of course, one of the ways that that more recently shows itself is in the ‘94 crime bill, which starts out here in California as California Three Strikes in February, and then becomes this national issue in September. California did it first, as I tell people, liberal old California, good old Cali, the state of the sunshine and the beach. Now, you wouldn’t think immigration was civil the way that they’re coming with the largest police forces ever between Customs and Border Protection and ICE, the detention prisons that are everywhere, and now the masked people, mainly men, that are running around grabbing people. You would not know this was a civil process, but it is civil. And so, it brings that racism, that anti-Blackness in particular, from this criminal punishment system into the immigration system, which is supposed to be civil, because Black people who are migrants are living right alongside Black people who are citizens. We’re all dealing with that over-policing. It’s not like they skip over and say, “oh my gosh, Miski, I see you’re not from here. Good for you, you know, continue going.”.\ And so, the over-policing, the over-charging, the over-sentencing, the coercive plea bargaining, all of these things lead to us being disproportionately imprisoned in the same ways that African-Americans are. The difference being that if you don’t have U.S. citizenship, then you find yourself now facing another system, which, again, is supposed to be civil but which has the same anti-Blackness that results in Black immigrants being 8% of the immigrant population, but 20% of those are facing deportation; which results in 76% of those Black people facing deportation because of criminal grounds. When you start looking at the Caribbean, those numbers spike: 98% of Jamaicans who are deported are deported on criminal grounds. And, of course, we know these criminal grounds don’t have to be anything serious. Generally speaking, if you get 25 to life or something, they’re not deporting you, they’re making you do your time, right? So all of that then has provided this space for more private prisons, because so many of these detention prisons are private prisons. More police in the form of ICE cops. More connection between ICE and immigration enforcement and local law enforcement through these 287G agreements with various county sheriffs. But also, at this point, just through the passage of laws, right? That is happening both on the federal level and on the state level. And what does that mean? As I said recently to a group of Black folks in Mississippi, raise your hand if you think you don’t look like you come from some other country, because I’m here to disabuse you of that. And so, whether you’re Black and they’re looking at you as a citizen, or you’re Black and they’re looking at you as an immigrant, you’re still being looked at as a Black person who they have the capacity to take up. We see the violations of people’s rights — completely disappearing people off the street by people who aren’t identifying themselves, grabbing people and separating them from family and community, even when they’re doing things like showing up for their court appearances as they’re supposed to do. This surveillance, where they’re just giving up all the information on people on Medicare, all the information on people who pay taxes, all this information is gonna come back and is already coming back to all of the people in this country. And so, I think it’s critical that we see what’s happening with immigration enforcement as the tip of the spear for the creation of this mega-police state that includes the National Guard, that includes the Marines, that includes all these entities that we see descending on DC after we saw that same dissent in Los Angeles that allegedly was immigrant focused. MN: To expand on that a little bit, can you talk to me a little bit more about the increased surveillance and its impacts on the carceral system and the targeting that Black people experience as a path towards criminalization. NG: It’s so interesting. I remember when they first started putting up cameras and people were thinking of them as a positive thing. Not everybody. But the description, the narrative, was that it was a positive thing. First, it was a positive thing because it was keeping people from running the light. I don’t know how the camera kept people from running the light. People are still running the light, they’re just on camera, but okay. Then they tried to make it seem like cameras are keeping people from stealing things, or from committing crimes. And again, cameras do not do any of that. All they do is just record people, collect people’s faces, and enable people to engage in facial recognition. Then slowly but surely people start to give up their rights, and it becomes normal for people to give up their rights. We see that in how people now are so willing, in the simplest of situations, to give up their rights. You go through the TSA line and they say, “stand here so we can take your picture.” People just stand there. But if you say, “I opt out,” they act like it’s a personal affront, like you just insulted their mothers or something. Sometimes they’ll actually fight with you, and then other people look around and are like, “oh, I don’t have to do this?” No, you don’t. You can opt out. But people are so used to the gathering of biometrics. It’s considered a normal thing to most folks, when actually I remember a time when people would have protested loudly and were protesting loudly. I’m thinking about this video I saw in DC where the National Guard and ICE and some other folks were walking through Georgetown. The look on those white people’s faces: classic. Classic. They were looking around — if you know Georgetown, D.C. — those white folks from Georgetown were looking around like, what part of the game is this? You didn’t hear these people were coming to DC? Oh, you just thought they were coming for Black people. Not you, right? And so I think it’s just critical that people are clearer about the ways in which surveillance that looks simple and looks like it’s just for these people over here, is actually where the test is. And then it becomes for everyone. So it’s important to make those connections. MN: Okay, so that was actually my last question for you. I think this is going to be so helpful for so many organizers. Thank you for your time. The Forge is built by and for organizers. articles.title: Zach Cregger Made a Resident Evil Movie With Bite
articles.author: Eileen Jones
articles.content: Zach Cregger’s horror-comedy Resident Evil is a real blast of a movie, fast, funny, scary, and inspired. Only an exuberant film lover could come up with such a gleefully inventive ninety-five-minute thrill ride as this one. I gather that Cregger is a fan of the Resident Evil video game franchise. That seems like the only possible explanation for why the acclaimed director of highly praised non-IP horror hits Weapons (2025) and Barbarian (2022), who presumably has a blank check to make any horror-related movie he wants, would choose to make the eighth Resident Evil entry in the twenty-four-year-old franchise. The reason certainly isn’t his love for the previous films. In an interview, he was unable to define what his version of Resident Evil is in relation to the rest of the movies — “A sequel? Prequel? Universe-expanding retro-reboot?” Cregger answered with a shrug. “I couldn’t really say. I’ve never seen one.” To Hell With the Franchise. Just Make a Good Movie. Fans of the films won’t like it, but I say this is the right attitude. Though some people claim that Cregger’s Resident Evil really conveys the sense of playing the game. Maybe it does. I don’t care. I don’t think it matters one single, solitary damn. I only care about how it plays as a stand-alone film, and as a stand-alone film, it’s delightful as hell. It stars Austin Abrams, who was so memorable as James, the addled young drug dealer living in a pup tent in the woods in Weapons . He plays Bryan, a harried twentysomething medical courier up against a crazily escalating series of gruesome attacks by “fucking monsters” as he tries to deliver an unidentified but urgent package to the remote rural Raccoon City hospital up in the wintry hills. Bryan is a callow young man in most ways, and perhaps not the sharpest knife in the drawer. But he brings an excessively dogged dedication to this courier job that makes him a comic example of Jean-Paul Sartre’s “bad faith” actor who’s allowed his identity to collapse into his professional role. Though there’s one complicating factor explaining his absolute desire to take on this last, voluntary delivery of the night: Bryan doesn’t want to go home. If he goes home, he has to have a serious face-to-face talk with his girlfriend, Michelle. She’s just discovered she’s pregnant, and she’s increasingly upset about Bryan’s glib answers on the phone that serve as a way to dodge any in-depth consideration of their relationship. It seems Bryan will face a thousand lab-created killer mutants on the loose rather than have that talk. Besides, delivering this package pays double Bryan’s usual rate. Given the grim economic times we live in, that’s motivation enough for most. There’s a glorious initial horror sequence — let’s call it the mountain road sequence — with so many lines of tension developing toward bloody disaster, the delirious viewer gets tied in knots just watching it. Bryan goes skidding up a heavily forested mountain road at night, his beat-up little car not equipped with the tire chains he’s been told are a necessity. In front of his meager headlights, the road fades into terrifying blackness. Michelle is on the phone with him, but at critical points in their angsty conversation, the reception keeps dying out. Just then — heart attack — a woman steps out from the snowy void right in front of him, and he brakes wildly but hits her anyway, tossing her up over the roof of his car. He swerves to a stop and gets out, horrified at what kind of gore he’s about to see. But all he can find are tracks in the snow heading off into the trees. Inadequately dressed in a puffy jacket and crappy sneakers, and relying on the thin light generated by his cell phone, he follows the tracks into the wilderness of trees, absurdly calling “Hello? Hellooooo?” He finds the woman, pale and staring, lying on her back, apparently alive but catatonic, with her contorted arms held out stiffly in front of her. As Bryan creeps up to her, we see him from her point of view, his head framed in the weird rectangle made by her arms. “Good gods,” I thought. “Cregger’s recreated the shot from Rashomon .” That’s Akira Kurosawa’s famous art film, released in 1950, which also serves as a dire referendum on Japanese culture post–World War II. In it, the complex central narrative commences when a woodcutter discovers a dead samurai in the forest. It’s a shocking event that will lead to an investigation and a series of deeply degraded, self-serving, and blatantly unreliable courtroom accounts about how the samurai died that indict a culture fallen into a moral abyss, and perhaps a humanity that’s truly irredeemable. And that’s the surreal shot from the dead samurai’s point-of-view, his reaching arms frozen in a state of rigor mortis framing the woodcutter’s face, that Cregger is evoking. A Darkly Comic Portrait of a Society at Collapse It’s both harrowing and funny for the 0.0000001 percent of the audience that gets the reference — film studies teachers everywhere will love it — because in an amusing genre-flick way, the reference is significant. This Resident Evil is creating a black comic portrait of a culture that’s probably past saving. The way people continue to follow their petty job descriptions and ignore the absolute catastrophe that’s staring them in the face — that’s soon biting and zombifying and mutating and consuming them — is summed up in Bryan’s stubbornly repeated lines, “That didn’t happen,” and “That wasn’t real.” But at the same time, it’s not ordinary people’s fault. As systems collapse all around them, a job these days is a hard-won lifeline. There are a lot of homages to other films — John Carpenter’s The Thing and Ridley Scott’s Alien are obvious ones — but many aren’t even references to other horror movies. For example, there’s the Die Hard –like scene when Bryan faces up to the fact that his situation is so desperate, he’ll probably never make it back to have that serious talk with Michelle. So via cell phone. he leaves an emotional apology and affirms his devotion to her in a heartfelt too-late-now message before he goes into the final climb up to the twenty-eighth floor of the Raccoon General Hospital building to deliver his package. And, like in Die Hard , he ends up doing it all without shoes. But back to the mountain road sequence. It goes on and on as a tour de force of pitiful human striving and error on Bryan’s part and increasing dread and nervous laughter for the audience. Bryan gets the catatonic woman into the car and tries to drive her to safety, ignoring her increasingly feral behaviors. Then he gets pulled over by an irritable local sheriff (Johnno Wilson) — relieved to offload the woman onto the police officer — and then all hell break loose on the road. Cregger keeps returning to deep-focus shots of the entire frozen landscape encompassed in the sequence, while adding new elements of terror into a frenzied chase involving a vicious dog that’s not just an ordinary dog, the wrecked and abandoned vehicles, the catatonic woman suddenly fully mobile and racing through the snow with animal speed, and Bryan’s sprints to a barn for shelter from weather and other, more urgent dangers. Then he tries to find sanctuary in a farmhouse, going from homely room to room and venturing up the dark, doomy stairs — yes, that’s Night of the Living Dead , folks. Far in the background, the flashing red-and-blue light bar on the police car is a haunting constant, a visual sign of urgency as well as a landmark indicating the spot where the surreal crisis state started for Bryan. It’s also an indicator of splendid filmmaking from start to finish, so good that the rest of the movie can’t quite live up to it. The catastrophic harm done by the biotech firm the Umbrella Corporation, which unleashed the experimental substance that infects and monstrously mutates whatever living beings come into contact with it, is ludicrously downplayed as a minor “human error” by its officious representatives, played by great comic actors Paul Walter Hauser and Zach Cherry. It turns out Bryan is carrying, instead of a kidney or other lifesaving organ to be transplanted, the “stabilizer” that can cure the infection and undo the mutations — it’s not just a McGuffin, it’s the solution to all the chaos! Even knowing how crucial his mission is can’t propel him to the top level of the hospital, however, when he finds out he’s expected to walk up all twenty-eight floors. It’s dangerous to take the elevator in a collapsing building blinking and buzzing with electrical shorts, a building which also happens to be teeming with kill-crazy mutants. But Bryan is dead-tired by the fourth floor. After all, how bad can the elevator be? You should go see the movie and find out. And without spoiling anything, it’s quite an ending! Cregger’s Resident Evil is an unexpectedly refreshing exercise in pure genre film entertainment, and it’s quite rightly doing gangbusters business . Cregger has done it again: he’s three for three now.

articles.title: German Centrists Are Smearing Die Linke as Antisemites
articles.author: Nimrod Flaschenberg
articles.content: Let’s be clear: Die Linke, Germany’s leading left-wing force, which resoundingly won Sunday’s elections in Berlin, is not an antisemitic party. It does not have an “antisemitism problem,” nor is it a menace to Jews in Germany or Berlin. While some Jews in the city perceive the Left as a threat, this perception is fueled by a false media narrative lacking a factual basis.That Die Linke is not a hotbed of antisemitism is obvious to anyone taking an honest look at the party: its leaders, its campaign methods, and the deep, sometimes overcharged embrace of Germany’s anti-antisemitism discourse which governs its rhetoric. Die Linke is committed to protecting Jewish life alongside a broader anti-racist vision. In this respect, it differs from mainstream German approaches to Jewish protection, which often treat the safety of Jews and the freedom of others as a zero-sum game.Die Linke has a large membership that is passionate about Palestinian solidarity and harshly critical of Israeli war crimes. Occasionally, activists express these views in ways unbefitting a democratic left-wing party, by making statements or using symbols that are seen as supporting armed resistance. This is an issue, and it’s at odds with the party’s democratically adopted resolutions on Israel and Palestine. A party must maintain a political line at its events and among its members. At the same time, these infractions do not reflect an antisemitic culture within the party.Are there antisemites in Die Linke’s midst? Certainly. Antisemitism exists across all segments of German society — native and migrant, young and old, Christian, Muslim, atheist, and even Jewish. There are also instances where anti-Israel positions escalate into antisemitism. Yet this is neither a structural nor an ideological problem. Polling suggests that antisemitic beliefs are actually more prevalent among voters of other parties. This is because left-wing politics, done right, combats all forms of discrimination and racism, including antisemitism.Why, then, was Die Linke Berlin attacked as antisemitic by rivals on both the Left and Right during this campaign? Because it was winning, and because smearing an entire organization based on the actions of a low-level member is the oldest trick in the book. This framing has a clear playbook, one frequently weaponized against socialist movements throughout history. It is also the exact tactic the Israeli right uses to delegitimize the Israeli radical left and Palestinian citizens of Israel.These attacks obviously failed. The Berlin public did not buy the narrative that Die Linke mayoral candidate Elif Eralp’s campaign was a smokescreen for Hamas. She won decisively on her agenda of affordability and political hope. This mirrors Zohran Mamdani’s campaign in New York City, where he was constantly questioned about Israel and Palestine despite focusing on bread-and-butter issues. In both cases, the media echo chamber’s insistence on centering foreign policy and antisemitism failed. Voters saw through the ploy. Depicting Eralp as a menace to Jews was particularly absurd, given her moderate positions on Israel-Palestine and her history of involvement in anti-antisemitism campaigns.However, these attacks were never meant to influence popular opinion. They were staged for this exact moment, after Die Linke had already won. The true goal was to make other progressive parties — the Social Democrats (SPD) and the Greens — hesitant to govern together with a party accused of antisemitism by mainstream German media and conservative Jewish institutions. The campaign targets Berlin’s political class to keep the Left out of power. This is done in the service of the real estate lobby, which objects to Die Linke’s signature policy of socializing Berlin’s apartment blocks.Hopefully, Die Linke’s democratic mandate is strong enough to make its role in government unquestionable. Nevertheless, attacks will likely continue throughout coalition negotiations and a future term in government. In these crucial moments, it is vital to avoid missteps.Once in power, it is critical that Die Linke put its values into action, ensuring Berlin remains a city that welcomes all communities and celebrates its diversity, including its disagreements. This requires genuine outreach to the Jewish community, which has been persuaded by national forces that it is at risk. Regardless of how unfounded these concerns may be, Die Linke has a responsibility to address them seriously, challenge false narratives where necessary, and truly make Berlin a city for all.

articles.title: On Canadian Militarism
articles.author: Rochester Red Star: News from Rochester DSA
articles.content: by Douglas Dollinger I thought my friends in ROC DSA might appreciate a bit of an update on your northern neighbour. What follows deals with the astounding rise of militarism in Canada under the Liberal prime minister Mark Carney. My American friends – I am myself half-American – will doubtless note some similarities between the rhetorical approaches of the Canadian and American governments, despite recent disagreements between the two countries and a flurry of ill-tempered threats by the American president against Canada. Mark Carney would have Canadians believe military spending is good for the economy. He is on track to move military spending from $70B this year (2026) to $150B in 2035, an astronomical increase. This, he has argued, will create all sorts of economic benefits for the Canadian people – a high rate of investment, good jobs, etc. He is dreaming. It has been amply documented by the Costs of War Project at Brown University, among others, that military spending creates fewer jobs per dollar spent than spending on education or health. But Trump whispered 5% and Carney and the Liberal Party jumped. Not out of sheer sycophancy, although sometimes I do wonder; no, Carney jumped because he is a neoliberal: Health care and education are costs; military spending is an investment. The distinction is a subtle one, granted. In other words, like most conservatives, he believes big government is bad, unless it comes in the form of policing, national security, business subsidies, financial bail-outs, and war-making. Like most conservatives, too, he committed the money without either campaigning on the increase or consulting Parliament. Of course, given that the opposition in Canada is the Conservative Party, which has never stopped whining about the cash-strapped military, Carney has faced almost no criticism from opposition leader Pierre Poilievre and his happy troupe of militarists. Interestingly, Carney recently announced the purchase of 12 submarines from Germany. These will be used, Canadian military analysts affirm, to “contain China” and protect the Canadian Arctic from Russians. Needless to say, however, it is the Americans who have actively challenged Canadian sovereignty over the Northwest Passage for decades, as the Laurier Centre for Military Strategic and Disarmament Studies has documented. This however can simply be forgotten. With fresh water becoming a highly endangered resource in many parts of the United States, it is a safe bet that American politicians will not sit on their hands and watch the Southwest become uninhabitable. Who has a lot of fresh water? Canada. If Canadian defence planners are aware of this looming danger, they seldom mention it; indeed, given the close integration of the Canadian and American military, it might be a bit much to expect the Department of National Defence even to consider the possibility. In all, Mark Carney has made no bones about building a war industry in Canada, taking up a proposal from his well-heeled friends at the Business Council of Canada, longstanding advocates of bolstering military spending in Canada. And so military Keynesianism is in full march. Carney’s record on Gaza, to address a related matter, would suggest he is only too happy to stand in the shadow of the American colossus, and so it is probable that the Canadian military will continue to serve as a kind of branch plant to the American military under the guise of NATO. Gaza is important here. If Canada cannot establish an independent stance on Gaza, it is difficult to conceive of its developing an independent stance on any critical geopolitical issue. Carney made the bold statement that Netanyahu would be arrested if he entered Canada, but just a few weeks back Netanyahu graced Canadian airspace and thus its territory with his august presence and Ottawa went dark. So much for the bold talk. It does not even seem clear that the Canadian government issued an objection, never mind scrambling the jets to force the Wing of Zion to alter its course. Meanwhile, as NATO moves east, Canada will have little choice but to jump on the ”contain China” bandwagon – indeed it was the American president who called for the 5% increase in the Canadian defence budget. Ever the Canadian stalwart, Carney obliged without hesitation. Note the refusal here to dignify the frequent threats to Canadian sovereignty by the American president. These can be dismissed for the most part for what they are, the deranged ejaculations of a political distemper called the Republican Party, but the American threat to Canada is nevertheless real. Those who believe the United States will respectfully acquiesce to Canadian sovereignty in the Arctic need to study American history. A country that can steal almost half of Mexico can certainly steal portions of the Arctic. Nor should anyone be surprised if this theft comes with the usual rhetorical embroidery about national security, which has become for all practical purposes the modern American substitute for Manifest Destiny. Carney talks big but carries a tiny stick, more twig than stick. Israel, again, provides a pertinent illustration. Despite the fact that just about all of the Jewish Holocaust experts in Israel have declared what is happening in Gaza a genocide, the Canadian government under Carney has not found its way to using the G-word, the best explanation for which is that it would ruffle American feathers, since it is the American government that has been cheerleading the genocide and otherwise supporting it without reserve. None of this can be mentioned: Canada must be a good partner and this means not stepping on the toes of the global hegemon. So much for Canadian independence and sovereignty. As the United States invades country after country – those foreign wars just keep happening for some inexplicable reason – Canada, hewing as always to the American line, courageously asserts that it is Iran that represents the source of international terrorism. Canadian officials utter such nonsense with a straight face. If knowledge is recollection, as Plato taught, then it becomes very hard not to see these individuals as heralds of an astonishing historical ignorance. Has Iraq been forgotten? What about Afghanistan? Vietnam? Nicaragua? Guatemala? Dominican Republic? Grenada? Panama? Libya? Laos? Cambodia? El Salvador? Yemen? Cuba? Haiti? Somalia? And now Iran. But no, you will not find a Canadian official in the government of Mark Carney with the courage to suggest, much less declare, that the United States has endorsed terror as a political instrument. The facts do not matter; they can be forgotten. Only a particularly deep form of ideological blindness can fail to see the terror standing behind what some Americans call “endless wars”. It is also this form of blindness that leads someone like Madeleine Albright, former American Secretary of State, to say that 500,000 dead Iraqi children – the documented result of Western sanctions on Iraq – was a price worth paying to bring down Saddam Hussein, a dictator whom the American government was only too happy to support when he was killing Iranians with American-supplied munitions, including chemical weapons. Canada voiced no objection. It is of course simply too impolite to point out that the American government supported Saddam Hussein for years. It crosses the ideological line and violates the bounds of what is considered serious and responsible political discourse. Power does many things: One thing it does quite well is to establish the limits of permissible discussion. Its most effective weapons in this respect are the words “terror”, “terrorists”, and “terrorism”. Three points should be noted here. First, the terrorist is always out there somewhere – in Iran, say, or Cuba, or China. Western nations, by contrast, never commit acts of terror. For instance, leveling Gaza, a small strip of land full of unarmed civilians, is not an act of terror, nor is Israel a terror state. The United States has been bombing Iran in what all acknowledge to be an illegal war, but no, it is simply the height of indecency to so much as suggest that the United States is practicing terror. Canada understands this and has not raised an eyebrow. Second, once a government has been dubbed a terrorist state, Western political leaders free themselves of any obligation to exercise diplomacy, since it is axiomatic that one cannot negotiate with terrorists. War becomes the one option left, which goes a long way toward explaining what otherwise remains a mystery to millions of Americans, the reality of endless wars. Third, once the label is attached to an official enemy, the military machinery of the West, and there is no greater in the world as Trump never tires of reminding us, can be brought to bear without moral scruples of any kind, and whatever horrors this produces – take a look at Gaza or Iraq for current examples – will be dismissed as a legitimate response to terror. Israel, remember, is only defending itself. In this regard, the West is always responding to terror but never committing it. The West, after stripping much of the globe of its valuable resources, enslaving millions of its inhabitants, and otherwise subjugating foreign peoples to regimes of terrible violence, has never suffered, so our leaders would have us believe, from an obsession with terror, with terror more specifically as a means of domination and control. Colonialism was an act benevolence, of kindness towards our darker brothers and sisters. For instance, the death of millions in India under the British Empire was either simply a mistake – a kind of huge clerical error – or it was an act of legitimate self-defence against restless, petulant, and ungrateful natives. The ideological mainstream in which people like Trump and Carney excogitate has little or no room for such reflections on Western terror. Nor is any thought given to what such pervasive violence might say about what we call Western values, meaning here not our espoused but our actual values, the ones that motivate our behaviour. Mark Carney wrote a book on values, so one might be tempted to think that he would be able to provide some useful guidance on what all of this might say about the values we hold dear; however, because he thinks inside the principal assumptions of the Washington consensus, he is as blind as a bat when it comes to identifying our actual values. There is thus little reason to expect any enlightenment from Mark Carney and the Liberal government of Canada. Canada once had a reputation – not altogether underserved – for its role as a peace keeper. Canada is now effectively Americanizing its approach to defence. Militarism has become the order of the day. The post On Canadian Militarism first appeared on Rochester Red Star .

articles.title: The US Gives Impunity to Israel and Sanctions Its Critics
articles.author: L. Canciello
articles.content: “It’s the first time, as a lawyer, I’m about to defend myself, not the people I work for.” Speaking as the United Nations’ Human Rights Council in Geneva discussed Palestine this March, Raji Sourani complained of attacks on human rights defenders’ most basic duties. Sourani, who is the director of the Palestinian Centre for Human Rights (PCHR), made these comments just after UN Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese had presented her report on systematic torture against Palestinians. For Albanese, torture is “the symbol of this genocide”: it devastates people’s bodies and dignity, while everything that makes Palestinians’ lives possible is being destroyed all around them. In a meeting on the sidelines of the session, Sourani, along with Issam Younis, who is executive director of Al Mezan, as well as representatives from Al-Haq, described what it means to continue documenting these crimes while their organizations are under US sanctions. Sourani explained how even though “the genocide continues as we speak,” he and his colleagues are forced to talk about frozen accounts and salaries they can no longer pay. “Instead of talking about genocide and ethnic cleansing, we’re here defending ourselves, with our silly little concerns: How can our organization survive and continue to defend human rights?” PCHR, Al Mezan, and Al-Haq are working with a specific legal purpose: collecting testimonies, assisting victims, and submitting evidence to the UN and the International Criminal Court (ICC). This is how violence suffered can become verified testimony and, ultimately, serve as evidence before a judge. But in this also lies the fundamental disconnect running through the UN meeting. While those who commit crimes still face no consequences, those who document them must weigh the consequences of every payment, trip, or collaboration they engage in. Archive Under Threat At Al-Haq’s offices in Ramallah, this work takes the form of an archive built up across a decades-long Israeli occupation. When we tried to get there from Bethlehem in July 2025, we got stuck in a long line at the checkpoint. An hour before our appointment, we still didn’t know if we’d make it. Every trip is subject to Israeli soldiers’ discretion. “We’ll get to Ramallah, inshallah ,” says our guide. Inside the offices, researchers have been collecting testimonies from across the occupied West Bank. Al-Haq keeps data on killings and demolitions, analyzes photographs and videos, and reconstructs attacks in order to challenge the official Israeli accounts. It has also created a forensic architecture unit, which uses spatial analysis and architectural tools to investigate human rights violations. “One of the things that motivates me to wake up every morning is that Israel seems to be running scared of our investigations,” says Mariam (who has been given a pseudonym), a researcher at Al-Haq. That fear, she explains, translates into pressure on funders and threats against banks. “They try to scare every single donor.” When an archive can refute the military’s version of events and contribute to international legal proceedings, it becomes a political threat. This is the evidence-gathering capacity that the sanctions now target. In truth, the attack on Al-Haq did not begin with the US sanctions. In 2021, Israel had already designated it and five other Palestinian organizations as terrorist. Then, in September 2025, Washington included Al-Haq, Al Mezan, and PCHR in the sanctions program established through Executive Order 14203 against the International Criminal Court. Assets under US jurisdiction were frozen, while US individuals and companies were prohibited from providing them with funds, goods, or services. Sanctions Program Since most international transactions are conducted in US dollars and through US-based platforms, many banks, donors, and partners in other countries severed ties despite not legally being required to do so. The report Criminalising Accountability refers to this as a mechanism of over-compliance. In less than a month, these organizations lost between 20 and 60 percent of their revenue, and YouTube removed over seven hundred videos, including witness accounts of torture and images of demolitions. For Al-Haq, this has meant staff left unpaid and US collaborators forced to resign. For Al Mezan, the sanctions compound the devastation in Gaza, affecting staff who’ve been displaced and the fate of researchers who must document events while also trying to protect their families, on top of their offices being hit. “We have no funds; we’ve had to cut salaries, and this has a direct impact on our ability to document crimes in Gaza,” says Younis. Albanese has also been personally sanctioned for her work as a UN special rapporteur. Her assets have been frozen and her transactions blocked, and she faces restrictions on entering the United States. When she takes the floor in Geneva, her first remark is directed at the institution that was supposed to protect her. Why, she asks, did the UN wait so long before discussing sanctions against one of its own special rapporteurs, against prosecutors and judges of the International Criminal Court, and against Palestinian organizations that cooperate with the justice system? Albanese says she has “less autonomy than [her] thirteen-year-old child. . . . just for writing reports to the United Nations” and is treated by the financial system like a “narcotrafficker, a drug dealer, or a terrorist.” What do she, the Palestinian organizations, and ICC officials have in common? They’re there “to pursue accountability, to advance justice for victims and survivors.” “Prosecutors cannot visit occupied Palestinian territory,” explains Sourani. They depend on organizations capable of reaching witnesses and preserving evidence. “When the Office of the Prosecutor, Palestinian organizations, judges, and the special rapporteur are targeted, the circle closes. The intention is clear.” Encouraged by Impunity The same selectivity permeates international institutions. In the UN Security Council, the permanent members’ veto power means there are often no consequences for violations. In the Human Rights Council, the same power dynamics determine which crises will lead to concrete measures and which instead remain a matter of only reports and resolutions. The ICC remains open, but it is isolated from the people who are gathering evidence and investigating. “We are witnessing the dismantling of accountability from the ground up,” warns Albanese. For Al Mezan’s executive director, Issam Younis, returning to the UN’s Palais des Nations holds personal significance. In 1993, he came here as a student to tell member states that Palestinians were being tortured. More than three decades later, the torture continues, and his organization is being sanctioned for its work with the ICC. “Governments no longer deny committing crimes,” he says. “In the past, they used to deny it. Now they’re proud to commit war crimes and genocide.” The images of Israel’s crimes, the official statements, and the many eyewitness testimonies have failed to provide protection. Indeed, this impunity is evident in the confidence with which the crimes are displayed: those who commit them are well-aware that the images will circulate and that other states will stand idly by. At the meeting in Geneva, a Palestinian lawyer recounted how detainees were forced to live for months inside a circle drawn on the floor, with their hands and feet chained, allowed to step outside it only for one-minute showers. “I’ve worked with prisoners for years. I’d never seen anything like it.” He described rapes, sexual violence, and amputations performed without anesthesia. “Torture does to the individual what genocide does to a group,” Albanese says. Documenting these acts does not restore to the victims what has been taken from them, but it preserves the possibility of recognition and justice being done. The lack of international action over Israel’s crimes in the West Bank has further consequences in the form of home demolitions, the seizing of land, and yet more attacks by settlers. Take what happened on July 28 last year in Umm al-Khair, when a bulldozer from a nearby Israeli settlement entered the village and damaged Palestinian property. Teacher Awdah Hathaleen, an activist and father of three, filmed the scene. In the videos, Israeli settler Yinon Levi raises his gun and fires in his direction. Awdah is fatally shot in the chest. Levi lives in the nearby settlement of Carmel. In 2024, he’d already been sanctioned by the United States, the European Union, the United Kingdom, and Canada for his role in violence against Palestinians. Yet the Trump administration revoked the US sanctions. After the killing, Levi was arrested and then quickly released again; Awdah’s body, however, was held for ten days, while conditions were imposed on the family regarding the funeral. “How can you release the murderer and hold onto the victim?” asks a representative of the Jerusalem Legal Aid and Human Rights Center. For Haneen Hathaleen, Awdah’s niece, what has changed since October 7, 2023, is above all the license with which the Israeli settlers act. In previous years, she says, the violence was at least partially restrained by fear of international backlash. Now that seems to have vanished. “After everything that happened in Gaza, no one has called Israel to account for anything,” she says. “So whatever they do here, who would dare oppose them?” The women of Umm al-Khair say that, since October 7, settlers have been coming almost every night. They enter the village, vandalize property, and prevent families from sleeping. “It’s not like it used to be,” they say. Fear is growing within the community that the increase in attacks will accelerate the displacement and annexation of their lands. The impunity for what is happening in Gaza is not separate from the West Bank: it strengthens the settlers’ conviction that they can act without resistance or consequences. Avenues of Accountability In an interview at the Café Suisse in the Palais des Nations, Palestinian Ambassador Ibrahim Khraishi tells me of the limitations of sanctions that target only individual settlers. Such measures, he argues, do not address the political and military system within which settlement violence is made possible and protected. They may restrict travel or freeze certain assets, but they do not stop the attacks or the expansion of settlements on the ground. Sanctions against those who document the violence are being expanded; sanctions against those who perpetrate the violence may be revoked or remain without concrete effect. In Umm al-Khair, impunity means that Awdah is killed, his body is withheld, and the attacks against his community continue. At the Palais des Nations, following the report on torture, some statements shift the debate from the evidence to Albanese herself: Hamas, accusations of antisemitism, and adherence to the code of conduct. The people documenting crimes must once again defend their legitimacy. “Diplomacy in times of genocide is not neutral,” Albanese responds. Younis insists that the UN member states need to take action: “Stop showing solidarity without taking action. It is time to act for accountability.” The tools exist. States that are parties to the ICC can defend the court’s work; the Netherlands can safeguard its operations; the EU can counter the effects of sanctions; and the UN can defend the special rapporteur to whom it has entrusted the mandate. Yet none of these actors has devised a response capable of protecting these people and institutions. The US government, through its control of the dollar, works to thwart accountability. But impunity is also fostered by states that acknowledge crimes and then refuse to use the tools that they have available to stop them. Many EU member states’ governments routinely claim that they stand up for international law, yet they maintain military, economic, and diplomatic relations with Israel without protecting the ICC or Palestinian organizations. Contagion Effect What is happening in Palestine will not remain confined to Palestine: impunity doesn’t just shield crimes that have already been committed but also makes future ones more likely. Every time a state sees another one disregard the courts, violate international norms, and pursue its own aims without paying the price, the rule of law loses strength elsewhere as well. The message to other governments is that rules can be set aside so long as they have political, military, or economic protection. This is how exceptional crimes come to set a precedent. This erosion is already evident in the growing challenge to international institutions. Chad has begun the process of withdrawing from the Rome Statute, a decision welcomed by Washington, which has called on other states to follow suit. According to Sourani, it would be a mistake to think that all of this concerns only Gaza or the Palestinians. Sanctions are replacing the rule of law with the “rule of the jungle.” “What is lost in Palestine will be lost everywhere,” warns Albanese. Meanwhile the genocide continues. The organizations that are supposed to collect and preserve evidence of it are being obstructed, deprived of funding, and isolated from international institutions. And even as the destruction continues in Gaza, settler attacks and pressure on Palestinian communities are mounting in the West Bank too. Yet while those who commit these crimes act with impunity, those documenting them are forced to defend their right to exist.

articles.title: The Left Should Start Using the Word “Evil”
articles.author: Susan Neiman
articles.content: Follow the news out of Washington for a week, and the usual vocabulary of political criticism starts to feel insufficient. Words like “authoritarian” and “illiberal” describe styles of governance. They say much less about what it is like to watch an administration indulge shameless sadism, pursuing cruelty for its own apparent enjoyment. The word that fits better is one many on the Left have trained ourselves not to use: “evil.” Our reluctance is not without reason. Evil calls to mind a Sunday school admonition or George W. Bush’s “axis of evil,” a phrase that helped sell the immoral and disastrous war on terror. A long materialist tradition treats moral ideas as downstream of economic realities and cautions against idealism that overly concerns itself with the questions of values and culture. Evil conjures childish boogeymen and unhelpful abstractions, not the social structures we want to seriously analyze. At the same time, the Left’s case for decent wages, housing, health care, and a world beyond class divisions is indisputably a moral case — whatever our theory says about the mechanics at play. And we don’t try to hide this: indeed, our movements often succeed best when we combine people’s self-interest with their sense of justice, neglecting neither. On some level, we know that we can’t do without the language of good. A new book, Call It Evil: Understanding the Trump Era by philosopher Susan Neiman, argues that we can’t do without the language of evil either, and that rejecting it has left us disarmed. Neiman contends that the Left has surrendered moral vocabulary to fundamentalists and in doing so has let a bleak theory of human nature pass for plain realism. She traces that theory to distorted readings of Adam Smith and Charles Darwin and to a deliberate, well-funded effort by American business to spread it. Neiman directed the Einstein Forum in Potsdam, Germany, from 2000 until earlier this year and has written about evil for decades, most notably in Evil in Modern Thought . Her other books include Learning from the Germans and Left Is Not Woke . In this interview, Neiman spoke with Kristen Ghodsee, a professor of Russian and East European studies at the University of Pennsylvania, author of Everyday Utopia , and a frequent contributor to Jacobin . Ghodsee and Neiman discussed why the Left needs moral language, and the perils of ceding it entirely to the people most likely to use it toward immoral ends. They also discussed where Neiman parts ways with many Marxists, how Germany’s official campaign against antisemitism became a crackdown on supporters of Palestinian rights, and the problems of essentializing any experience, including that of class. Kristen R. Ghodsee The title of your book enjoins us to use explicitly moral language to describe politics in the Trump era. You suggest that many on the Left feel uncomfortable using words like “good” or “evil” or “truth” because of their religious connotations. Why is the language of morality necessary to the Left, especially in this political moment? Susan Neiman It’s common to condemn the Trump administration’s contempt for the rule of law. We forget that the rule of law only works if people commit to upholding it even if a legal decision goes against their self-interest — and that’s a moral commitment. James Madison knew that even the best constitution was no protection without “virtue in the people.” The Founding Fathers were less averse to moral concepts than we have become, especially on the liberal left. Let’s dispense with a widespread misunderstanding that good and evil are religious ideas. Moral intuitions precede theology. Religion is a response to the problem of evil, though I don’t think it’s a very successful one. Every culture recognizes evil, whatever their religious practices. You could call it “awareness of injustice.” That’s something that children, most primates, and according to one study, even rats display. My favorite argument that morality precedes religion comes from the Bible itself, when Abraham urges God not to punish the innocent with the guilty — not to accept collateral damage. That suggests that even should you have a direct line to the Lord himself, he isn’t the source of your moral judgment. It’s true that religious believers are more comfortable using moral concepts, and it’s equally true that fundamentalists abuse them. But why should we allow the most powerful tools in our language to be appropriated by those who are least able to use them responsibly? People are moved by those concepts, which appeal to deep intuitions and emotions; better to learn to analyze evil than deny what we can see every day. If the cold-blooded murder of fishermen, or schoolgirls, or peacefully protesting demonstrators isn’t evil, what is? Words like “authoritarian” are simply too weak to do it justice. I don’t think Zohran Mamdani uses the word “evil,” but his campaign was premised on moral values, and its success cannot be reduced to affordability. He leaned hard on questions of justice, in particular the injustice that most people who keep New York City running cannot afford to live there. And his steadfast condemnation of the genocide in Gaza — which initially seemed a huge liability — is a great source of his popularity. We’re so used to politicians abandoning their principles when it suits them that Mamdani’s display of integrity became a source of credibility, creating hope he won’t sell out on other issues. We should also remember that the most successful (albeit only partially so) leftist movement in US history was the civil rights movement, which roused millions of people through a clear moral message. Kristen R. Ghodsee Although written in clear and accessible prose, this short book grapples with complex philosophical issues. It forces readers to confront some of the most vexing theoretical issues of leftist politics over the last two centuries. Haunting this debate are the specters of Immanuel Kant and G. W. F. Hegel and the perennial tension between idealism and materialism. For you, Marxism is far too wedded to the idea that the economic relations of production determine our superstructural concepts of good, evil, justice, love, and so on. Why should the Left reclaim the power of ideas in its pursuit of progressive change? Susan Neiman Most of my work has been devoted to making complex philosophical issues accessible to general audiences, since I believe philosophical assumptions are a greater part of our lives than we recognize. Take statements like “Be realistic” or “That’s just human nature.” As used in ordinary language, they imply a web of assumptions about the world we take for granted because we haven’t reflected on them. Materialism is one of the most basic. Like anyone who learned from Karl Marx, I’ve spent hours in arguments about differences between materialism, dialectical materialism, and historical materialism, whether there are major differences between the early and late Marx, and how to get around the fact that his nineteenth-century predictions did not hold up. A long seminar wouldn’t do those arguments justice, much less a short interview. Bertolt Brecht’s dictum “First comes the grub, and then come the morals” is chronologically correct. When people are hungry or homeless, they don’t have much energy to reflect on morality. Once their stomachs stop rumbling, they begin to think about justice. Marxism’s biggest paradox is that it inspires people through demands for justice — i.e., moral claims — while theoretically undermining the basis of that inspiration. Ideas move people in powerful ways — often rather bad ones, as nationalism today shows. I admire the misread and forgotten Eduard Bernstein , a founder of the German Social Democratic Party. Although he was Friedrich Engels’s literary executor, he rejected dialectical materialism, which he thought was an insult to workers, who were just as capable of being moved by ideals as anyone else. He was also an early feminist and supporter of gay rights. Bernstein wrote that “social democracy needs Kant, who shows that materialism is the most deceptive ideology, and that contempt for ideals, the elevation of material facts to omnipotent powers is simply deceptive.” The Enlightenment is now so dismissed that it’s often forgotten that Marxism was once seen as the culmination of Enlightenment thought — both by its defenders in the Soviet Union and the German Democratic Republic, for example, and by its Nazi opponents. On that view, Marx’s contribution was to insist that the ideals of the Enlightenment demand material realization — not that those ideals were reducible to material interests. It’s a subtle but important difference. Call It Evil argues that we’ve been conditioned to accept materialism as a fact , not an ideology. The idea that moral concepts are just superstructure is supported by crass misreadings of Adam Smith and Charles Darwin, reinforced by Michel Foucault . I show how these misreadings of Smith and Darwin created a sense of inevitability you can read in any newspaper, without ever asking whether they are debatable philosophical assertions. Since the end of the Cold War, the sense of inevitability has become stronger. Kristen R. Ghodsee Most secular people today imagine evil as something diabolical, but Hannah Arendt talked about the “banality” of evil. You also wrote a groundbreaking book, Evil in Modern Thought , exploring the concept’s dimensions. Many Marxists would argue that our social conception of “evil” emerges from the base of our material experience of the world, but you suggest that there is a kind of Platonic form of pure evil that exists independently of our social realities. That’s why we know it when we see it and why it’s such a powerful concept. Can you talk about your use of this word? What is the rhetorical power of “evil,” for instance, over “awful”? Susan Neiman You can measure the rhetorical power of “evil” by the number of people — mostly on the Left — who object to it. It’s striking how many point out that it’s a dangerous term that can be abused, as if that had never occurred to anyone who’s thought about the subject. “Awful” can apply to a filthy apartment or a bad boyfriend. If it’s all you have to say about a genocide, you have failed to grasp what genocide is. I’m not a Platonist, and I don’t believe that evil exists independently of social realities. Until the mid-eighteenth century, most people did. I do believe that it’s something we recognize and can learn to recognize better. Arendt’s work was crucial in showing us that the most dangerous forms of evil emerge not from sadism or cruelty but from our tendency to go along with systemic structures around us and not rock any boats that might disturb our lives. That she turned out to be wrong about the man Adolf Eichmann, as was proven by tape recordings that were unknown in 1963, doesn’t undermine the validity of her claims. Genocide cannot be committed by a few consciously evil people alone. It requires millions who accept them. Kristen R. Ghodsee As I read your book, I kept thinking about David Graeber and David Wengrow’s The Dawn of Everything and how many contemporary debates about capitalism and socialism lean heavily on different conceptions of “human nature.” You show how American conservatives used their money and influence to fund the creation of think tanks and university programs in neoliberal economics and evolutionary psychology to protect their economic interests. Through their foundations and societies, they propped up men like Milton Friedman who asserted that all societies are based on greed and self-interest. Do you think that conservatives are somehow more effective at weaponizing ideas than progressives, and if so, why? But also, given that these ideas were promoted by those most likely to financially gain from them, isn’t this a textbook case of the economic base determining the superstructure? Susan Neiman I found Graeber and Wengrow’s book liberating, though I wish they’d given Jean-Jacques Rousseau more credit. His argument should be music to their ears: we have no access whatsoever to the deeds, much less the thoughts and drives, of our prehistoric ancestors, so we project conceptions of human nature onto the past that suit our political projects. The Dawn of Everything was important for that argument; another related book is Stefanos Geroulanos’s The Invention of Prehistory . You cannot defend socialism without questioning the conception of human nature that capitalist ideology has taught us to take for granted. Everyone reading these words has surely encountered people who insist that socialism is nice in theory, but human nature ensures that it can’t work in practice. When I began work on this book, I assumed that the various ways this ideology is blasted at us were just unfortunate coincidences; everything else seemed too conspiratorial. Looking further, particularly at Naomi Oreskes and Erik M. Conway’s excellent The Big Myth: How American Business Taught Us to Loathe Government and Love the Free Market , I realized how deliberate the mythmaking has been. Certainly, economic interests can play a huge role in shaping and spreading ideologies. I’m just denying that they always determine them. And you’re right that conservatives are better at promoting ideas than leftists; a classic of mid-twentieth-century conservatism was called Ideas Have Consequences . Once leftists acknowledge that they do, we’ll get better at defending them. Kristen R. Ghodsee Your wonderful chapter on propaganda starts with an anecdote about moving to Berlin in 1982 and listening to East and West German news broadcasts. What did these broadcasts teach you? Why do you think Americans are so particularly bad at recognizing propaganda? And why do you think propaganda erodes our capacity for moral judgment? Susan Neiman Those broadcasts were great background for reading Noam Chomsky and Edward Herman’s Manufacturing Consent , published a few years later. It’s not that I suddenly believed everything the East Germans broadcast, but I understood how context and framing, even without deliberate lying, could create completely different takes on reality. The experience also inoculated me against a later lie, namely that the West Germans did a better job of dealing with the Nazi past than the East Germans. It’s a West German myth now accepted in much of the world. Few West Germans were spreading that myth in the 1980s, since anyone with basic knowledge of German could tell it was the East, at the time, that was reckoning with the Nazis — incompletely, but far more than the West, which wanted to sweep that history under the carpet. That’s a useful lesson for thinking about Cold War America as well. Americans are bad at recognizing propaganda because our biggest piece of propaganda is that we have none. Possibly a silver lining of Trump’s attack on the media, and the media’s complicity with it, is that Americans will better recognize how worldviews can be shaped by political interest. I fear, however, that his weaponization of the phrase “fake news” leads people in a different, nihilistic direction: there is no news that isn’t manipulated to maintain power. I don’t think we can have real moral judgment without considering competing views. We might accidentally behave morally, but it isn’t judgment if it isn’t reflective, and that means not taking your own morality for granted. It’s much easier to reflect if you are confronted with different moral and political assumptions. Too few Americans have opportunities to do that. Kristen R. Ghodsee In your chapter on why Gaza matters, you walk back some of the claims you made in your previous book, Learning from the Germans . What happened in Germany after October 7, 2023, that made you see things differently? Susan Neiman The problems started before October 7; they came to a head in 2019, when the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party proposed a parliamentary resolution banning Boycott, Divestment, and Sanctions (BDS). It was a brilliant and sinister form of — can I call it Jew-washing? By embracing the government of Israel, the AfD hoped to answer charges of neofascism. How could it be fascist if it unconditionally supports the State of Israel? It also advances one of its main goals, which is keeping Muslim immigrants out of Germany. No one challenged it, because the other parties were afraid to be seen as less philosemitic than the AfD, so they immediately passed a similar resolution, which resulted in canceling artists, writers, journalists, and others who can be described as “close to BDS,” i.e., anyone who supports Palestinian rights. And many of us are Jewish. This created the biggest political/cultural debate of the last six years, which took place in television, radio, in print, and in parliaments. Learning from the Germans had argued that Germany’s historical reckoning was flawed, but it did better than any other country in facing the evils of its past history. The recent debates exposed the depth of those flaws in ways that forced me to revise my views. German reckoning suggests that as long as one is nice to Jews, any Jews, one has done one’s duty in opposing Nazism. This is an extremely simplistic understanding of fascism, ignoring the real lesson of Nuremberg: the importance of upholding human rights, and that they apply to all humans — including Palestinians. Kristen R. Ghodsee You also write about how the far right has weaponized antisemitism, not only Trump in his attacks on US universities but also Alternative for Germany, which recently won almost 44 percent of the vote in the state of Saxony-Anhalt. What does what you term “philosemitic McCarthyism” look like in practice? Susan Neiman The AfD provides a perfect example, but it is not alone. In 2022, I cohosted a conference in Berlin, Hijacking Memory , examining the weaponization of antisemitism among right-wing parties in seventeen countries. Predictably, the press accused us of antisemitism. The reception illustrated the problem we were analyzing! People have been fired from jobs and had projects, exhibits, or appearances canceled. Those hardest hit are Muslims and people of color who support them. Americans will see parallels in the second Trump administration. What’s particularly infuriating for leftist Jews like me is this: Even if they don’t give a damn about Palestinians, why in the world do they think these kinds of repression protect Jews? On the contrary: targeting other groups, allegedly to protect us, only increases antisemitism. If I were paranoid, I’d suspect a conspiracy. Kristen R. Ghodsee In your chapter on woke identity politics, you warn that leftists should not replace racial essentialism with class essentialism. While social classes are obviously fluid and we all have multiple allegiances, don’t you think there is a profound difference between those of us who must work for a living versus those who can live off the dividends and capital gains generated by their (often-inherited) wealth? There is a real bifurcation between the owners of capital (and their heirs) and the rest of the population who must sell their time, labor, or attention to survive, the so-called 99 percent. How can any universalism encompass the billionaires? Susan Neiman I agree with Mamdani that there’s no good reason for billionaires to exist. Apart from die-hard ascetics, most of us who work for a living can imagine a luxury or two we wish we could afford. But it’s impossible for anyone to buy a billion dollars’ worth of treats; the point of making that much money is to exercise political power, as billionaires are doing with increasing shamelessness. Particularly given how much of their wealth depends on other people’s labor, that’s an injustice that cancels any form of democracy. There are profound differences between those who live on dividends and those who work for a living, just as there are profound differences between men and women, and between people of different ethnicities. Those are differences in experience, which is why it’s so important for different voices to be heard, but essentializing those differences is a metaphysical mistake with dangerous political consequences. And the notion of class has changed so much since Marx’s day that it’s unhelpful to depend on it; far better is a universal conception of justice, which occasionally moves even members of the ruling class to action. Where would we be without Engels’s dividends? Kristen R. Ghodsee You end by claiming that socialism offers a way out of the morass we find ourselves in today. Can you talk about your vision of socialism? Susan Neiman In my last book, Left Is Not Woke , I offered a normative definition of what it (should) mean to be left today. There are three principles common to both leftists and liberals: We are universalists, not tribalists, because we believe that genuine connections and obligations do not depend on origins. We believe in a principled distinction between justice and power, even though the distinction is often abused. We believe that progress toward more just and fulfilling societies isn’t inevitable, but it is possible. In that book, I argued for a popular front between leftists and liberals in a time of rising fascism. But there’s a fourth principle that distinguishes leftists from liberals: Social rights — to health, education, housing, fair labor practices, and leisure — are not “benefits” or “safety nets” but rights as important as political rights to speak, vote, travel, or worship as we please. Like Bernstein, I think those rights could be achieved through democratic processes. I’m well aware that this can look utopian at this moment. My book is meant as a contribution to the conceptual changes that must happen for a peaceful revolution to take place. In a world that’s armed to the teeth, anything else is too dangerous.

articles.title: Far-right Victory in German State Elections Shocks the Center
articles.author: MLToday
articles.content: By Ana Vracar, Breakthrough News September 7, 2026 The far-right AfD won Saxony-Anhalt’s state election on September 6.
