Progressive analysts link results to mainstream neoliberal policy failures. The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) secured a convincing victory in the Saxony-Anhalt state election on September 6, 2026. The election was marked by a high turnout of nearly 78% and took place amid a climate of widespread anger against federal policies implemented by the Merz administration – particularly attacks on social services and welfare, and ongoing militarization. The AfD won approximately 44% of the vote, more than double its result in the 2021 election. Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU) saw its support halve to barely over 17%, followed by the Social Democrats (SPD), the Greens, and the progressive party Die Linke – all recording less than 10% of the vote. The Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) crossed the 5% electoral threshold. Despite the result, it remains unclear whether the far right will be able to form a government, as mainstream parties have historically maintained a “firewall” against cooperation with the AfD. For his part, AfD state leader Ulrich Siegmund indicated the party’s preference is forming a non-coalition administration, even if it means going to the polls again. He assured that, in that case, the AfD would win over 50% of the vote. While mainstream parties across Germany expressed shock over the election result, critics on the left argue this is the result of their own unwillingness to break with neoliberal policies and attacks on labor rights. Ever since the far right began to record stronger electoral results, the mainstream parties’ focus has remained almost exclusively on the AfD’s anti-immigrant discourse , even embracing growing chunks of this narrative in an attempt to preserve votes. These same parties fail to recognize the importance of the cost of living crisis and massive job losses for voters. The fear of not being able to make ends meet was one of the top concerns in Saxony-Anhalt. This indicated that many votes for the AfD were cast in the attempt to find an alternative to the mainstream. Merz’s administration , however, is apparently still oblivious to these concerns. The AfD coming into power would also not translate into a change of economic policy, considering their program remains aligned with neoliberal principles . While this leaves room for the left to act and shape a socially just strategy, notable social mobilizations are yet to be fully recognized as pointers for progressive parties. AfD’s success has been noted with concern by progressive politicians across the region. They pointed to the stubborn insistence of mainstream parties on austerity policies even as it becomes apparent that they are pushing people into the arms of the extreme right. “The far right is back in Germany,” French presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon reacted. “This is a catastrophic demonstration of the blindness of Europe’s centrist politicians. The disaster is of their making.” “Things didn’t turn out well under the far right last time, and they won’t this time either,” echoed Slovenian progressive party Levica . “The only answer to the consequences of capitalism is socialism.” The post Far-right Victory in German State Elections Shocks the Center appeared first on MLToday .

articles.title: Middle Class or Working Class?
articles.author: MLToday
articles.content: By Greg Godels September 16, 2026 The Pew Research Center provides a vast amount of information on US citizens through polling and surveys. Of course, it is imperative that those of us digesting that information understand the biases and misrepresentations that can distort or slant their findings. It is essential that the wording of queries, the choice of descriptions, and the connotations of words and phrases be carefully weighed before accepting Pew’s findings. Among the more useful and telling surveys are those that show how people change their self-description over time– how they see themselves differently under different circumstances. And likely one of the most interesting of those many possible self-descriptions is membership in a social class. Now social classes are notoriously difficult to define. Problems loom immediately. One, it is extremely difficult to decide how to characterize a social class. What the most important factors are in distinguishing meaningful, useful social groups is not obvious or easy to discern. Arbitrary or artificial classes are seldom of significant import: the sophisticated and unsophisticated, the left-handed and right-handed, generations X, Y, and Z. Two, it is necessary to ground social classes in something objective– perception of social status must be distinguished from the actual state of people. The class that people think they occupy is less important than what position that they actually occupy. Social class must be scientifically determined and not determined by custom, authority, or prejudice. Three, significant sets of people grouped as classes should be relatively discretely determined– who is inside and who is outside should have relatively sharp boundaries. Few discussants of class address or meet these standards of rigor, including the Pew Research Center. They arbitrarily define class based upon household income, distinguishing an upper, middle, and lower class. For Pew, the middle class is defined as “those with an income that is two-thirds to double that of the U.S. median household income, after incomes have been adjusted for household size.” The upper class and lower classes are defined accordingly as above and below the middle class. Certainly, Pew’s definition is objective and sharply defined, but questionably useful and decidedly arbitrary. Without mounting a stout defense– in this context– and without demonstrating its vitality, I would offer the Marxist class definitions as a robust alternative meeting all standards: division into the working class and the bourgeoisie. For Marxists, the determining features of social class are grounded in socio-economic relations. One set of actors, the bourgeoisie, is determined by their owning and/or controlling of the productive assets of a society. And the other set of actors, the working class, is determined by their lack of those assets and their consequent necessity to seek employment from asset-holders or the state. That is not to say that there cannot be problems with the Marxist definition, but it remains the most productive framework to understand class-based social behavior. Nevertheless, the Pew surveys provide an insightful and useful look at how the working class has changed and how it sees itself. Since the early Cold War and the decimation of the left-leaning trade unions by means of the betrayal and co-option of militant class-based unionism, bankrupt and corrupted union leaders and their politician counterparts have tried to sell the idea that workers were “middle-class.” This elusive and deceptive term served them well, giving the idea that workers had climbed from the lower class to a much higher, more stable, and “typical” status. Achieving the middle class meant enjoying the good life and signaled that success of the capitalist system for workers. To the extent that workers bought the idea of middle-class status, they accepted the notion that they could do no better and that alternative visions were unnecessary, even undesirable. Thus, the very concept of the middle class and the argument that most workers were in it became a powerful ideological tool in the fight against Communism and other alternative paths. Consequently, ideologues, the commentariat, politicians, and labor leaders were and are energetically resolved to defend it. A finding by the Pew Research Center in November, 2024 must have sent shock waves through this cabal of apologists for capitalism: The share of Americans who are in the middle class is smaller than it used to be. In 1971, 61% of Americans lived in middle-class households . By 2023, the share had fallen to 51%, according to a new Pew Research Center analysis of government data. As a result, Americans are more apart than before financially.… [T]he growth in income for the middle class since 1970 hasn’t kept pace with the income growth for the upper tier and the share of total U.S. household income held by the middle class has plunged. Not only do a smaller share of Americans live in middle-class households today, the incomes of middle-class households have also not risen as quickly as the incomes of upper-income households. While the Pew definition of “middle class” is demonstrably bias-laden and misleading, it nonetheless shows an objective, statistical decline in the status of many workers in the statistical middle. Pew is forced to conclude: “The share of total U.S. household income held by the middle class has fallen almost without fail in each decade since 1970.” This cannot be good news to the staunch defenders of the benefits of US capitalism. If defenders of capitalism find this finding threatening, what must they think of the findings of a more recent poll? A report in August concludes that “Most Americans think of themselves as “working class” today: Overall, 60% of U.S. adults say the term describes them well. And the identity is widely adopted by people across all income and educational groups – including half of both Americans who have a bachelor’s degree and those who are upper income.” (Pew emphasis) Clearly, the fact that so many US respondents describe themselves as working class must disappoint the hucksters hustling the notion that the US is the land of a vast and socially content middle class. And further, the fact that these self-descriptions as working class largely cross over other common descriptive categories– sex, race, education, and income– should put to rest most of the Internet prattle over an uneducated white working class. While the numbers may vary, a majority of people in nearly all significant categories but the very rich identify as working class. Does this also mean that most people understand social class in a way not so different from the Marxist definition? Pew researchers are surprised that “50% of Americans who consistently pay their bills in full, have several months of emergency savings and report being able to meet their expenses comfortably, say they consider themselves to be working class.” The lesson of this survey is not just for those who purvey “middle class” snake oil to convince people that we all sacrifice and gain equally in the best of all societies. There is a lesson for the left here as well. For those who have written off workers as “aristocrats of labor,” as lacking in class consciousness, as identifying with the rich and powerful, there is more than a little possibility of kindling a new class politics. There is an opportunity to place working-class interests before people who, in fact, identify as workers. That has always been the role of Socialists and Communists. A guest on a fairly prominent left podcast recently stated emphatically that the sole goal of the left in the advanced capitalist countries should be to show solidarity with the downtrodden in the Global South. Unfortunately, that is a belief shared by far-too-many on the left. While that goal is and should always be a necessary aim for the left, it should be remembered that class struggle– the awakening and empowering of our working class– is both the essence of socialist politics and the most effective way of influencing the fate of the international victims of our capitalist class. As affirmed in the Marxist canon, The Communist Manifesto, “The proletariat of each country must, of course, first of all settle matters with its own bourgeoisie.” Class consciousness is alive and well. The excuse that US workers are too backward to understand who they are– an underlying assumption of many self-described Marxists– stands refuted. The post Middle Class or Working Class? appeared first on MLToday .

articles.title: CP Venezuela Denounces Rodriguez Government’s Handover of Oil Wealth to the US
articles.author: MLToday
articles.content: September 2, 2026 Statement by the Political Bureau of the Central Committee of the Communist Party of Venezuela (PCV) concerning the Venezuela-U.S oil deal: “The Political Bureau of the Central Committee of the Communist Party of Venezuela (PCV) categorically rejects this latest and serious transfer of national assets carried out by the illegitimate and illegal triumvirate that holds de facto power in Venezuela. Information that has come to light in recent days confirms the transfer of one-fifth of Venezuela’s oil reserves to U.S. companies through agreements negotiated behind the backs of the Venezuelan people, without transparency, and outside the constitutional controls that must govern any operation involving the Republic’s strategic interests. Delcy Rodríguez confirmed the transfer of 17 strategic oil fields with approximately 65 billion barrels of proven reserves. According to the list that has circulated, not all of these are exclusively virgin fields. The agreement provides for new developments in fields where oil reserves have already been proven and where operational knowledge has been accumulated over decades. This is neither a minor agreement nor a simple commercial transaction. We are witnessing the transfer of a significant portion of the nation’s primary wealth under conditions unknown to the country and regarding which there has been neither the necessary public debate nor the parliamentary oversight established in Articles 150 and 187 of the Constitution. Once again, fundamental matters of Venezuelan political and economic life are announced from the White House, and Miraflores [the presidential palace] simply goes along with it. According to reports that have circulated following Donald Trump’s announcement, the U.S. Department of War would have a direct stake in these oil projects through companies linked to their development. This fact reveals with absolute clarity the nature of the new relationship that is being imposed on Venezuela. We are not dealing with converging interests between two countries negotiating on terms of equality and mutual respect. We are dealing with a U.S. policy aimed at securing its own energy, economic, and strategic interests through increasing control over Venezuelan resources. Trump himself, who has described the agreement as “a gift,” has made it clear that he intends to use Venezuelan crude oil to meet U.S. energy needs, including the replenishment of its strategic reserves. Thus, Venezuelan oil—the heritage of our people—will end up fueling the U.S. economic and military machine. Venezuelan oil is becoming a strategic resource in the service of U.S. imperialism’s global supremacist ambitions, underpinning its warmongering plans and the terrorist expansionism of Israeli Zionism. Delcy Rodríguez claims that national sovereignty has been preserved. However, her invalid amendment to the Organic Law on Hydrocarbons proves exactly the opposite. The reform pushed by the triumvirate opens the door for transnational corporations not only to have operational control over strategic oil projects but also to participate directly in fundamental decision-making regarding the exploitation of the nation’s resources. Added to this is an unprecedented dismantling of the tax system. The new legislation eliminates and relaxes a series of tax obligations and reduces the financial commitments of private companies that will participate in the oil business. While the Venezuelan people are subjected to meager wages, deteriorating public services, and growing difficulties in meeting their basic needs, transnational capital is offered extraordinarily favorable conditions to appropriate an ever-increasing share of the nation’s oil wealth. The situation is particularly shameful for those who, for years, built their political discourse around the defense of national sovereignty and the denunciation of U.S. imperialism. The triumvirate has ended up subordinating national economic policy to the needs of its own political survival. Today, they act as the White House’s lackeys. They can no longer accuse those of us who denounce this reality of playing into the hands of imperialism. Today, the White House has become a central hub for fundamental decisions regarding Venezuela’s political and economic life, while the illegitimate triumvirate carries out and ensures its agenda. The PCV reminds the triumvirate that Article 138 of the Constitution of the Republic establishes with absolute clarity that “any usurped authority is ineffective and its acts are null and void.” Those who exercise power without due constitutional legitimacy cannot, with impunity, compromise the nation’s assets or mortgage the future of the Venezuelan people. The PCV condemns this savage plundering, now presented with technocratic rhetoric intended to give a false appearance of rationality and legality to the brazen looting of the national heritage. For years, the authoritarian leadership of the PSUV used criminal sanctions and the blockade as mechanisms to operate in secrecy, evade controls, and enable the illegal enrichment of privileged sectors at the expense of the suffering of millions of Venezuelans. Now it seeks to use the rhetoric of “pragmatism” to justify a new phase of surrender. The Venezuelan people cannot accept that the national crisis be used as an excuse to hand over the country’s strategic resources to foreign corporations. Venezuela’s recovery demands transparency, sovereignty, democratic control, and popular participation. It demands the restoration of institutional frameworks, the full reinstatement of the Constitution, and the return to the Venezuelan people of their right to decide the fate of their resources. In the face of plunder, surrender, and subordination, the PCV reaffirms its commitment to the consistent defense of national sovereignty, democratic rights, and the interests of the working class and the people. This historic moment demands that we move forward with the broadest possible popular, patriotic, democratic, and anti-imperialist unity. No to the surrender of Venezuelan oil! For the restoration of constitutional order and the full sovereignty of the Venezuelan people!” The post CP Venezuela Denounces Rodriguez Government’s Handover of Oil Wealth to the US appeared first on MLToday .

articles.title: Macklemore Controversy Creates an Uproar on Social Media
articles.author: MLToday
articles.content: By Michael Scheinberg and Walter Tillow September 20, 2026 The banning of the hip hop artist Macklemore from Ed Sheeran’s The Loop musical tour at the insistence of billionaire Robert Kraft, and the pushback and criticism this gross act of censorship has engendered show the growing strength of the movement in solidarity with Palestine. Below we post Macklemore’s statement. To us, it calls to mind a statement made by Paul Robeson in the 1950s during the worst days of McCarthyism about the artist’s responsibility . Robeson said: “Every artist, every scientist, every writer must decide now where he stands. The artist must take sides. He must elect to fight for freedom or for slavery. I have made my choice. I had no alternative.” The Macklemore statement: “I’m not sure how to start this. So I’m going to speak from the heart and share the truth. Ed Sheeran and his team have made the decision to remove me from The Loop tour. But before I get into it, I want to say something that should be obvious. In this moment I think it matters. I am not a victim. Ed Sheeran is not a victim. Pink is not a victim. We have careers, money, opportunities, safety and audiences around the world. Whatever consequences any of us face for what we say, we get to go home to our families. The victims are the Palestinian people. The men, women and children who have been killed, starved, displaced and forced to live through unimaginable violence. More than 20,000 children have been killed in Gaza alone. People are being killed today, and people will be killed tomorrow. I want to make sure that as I tell this story, we don’t lose sight of that. Ed is my friend. I’ve known him for 13 years. We’ve shared late nights, studio sessions and stages. He has this infectious magic about him that I’ve grown to love. I consider him a brother. And because of that, we’ve had some difficult conversations this past week. The type of talks rooted in love and respect for one another that still end in a place of fundamental disagreement. Nothing I’m writing here is out of spite or because I want to tear down his character. But as I told Ed multiple times on the phone, our friendship can’t change my responsibility to tell the truth about what happened. Last Monday, in the middle of all the media attention surrounding Pink and what I said at MetLife, Ed told me that Robert Kraft called him. We were scheduled to play Gillette Stadium later this month, which is owned by the Kraft Group. Ed told me that Kraft said I would not be allowed to perform in his stadium. Ed also told me that Kraft had rallied some of the other stadium owners and collectively they gave him an ultimatum: if Macklemore stays on the tour, you will not be allowed to play in our venues. Ed was in a fucked up position. He knew it. His typical apolitical stance was being challenged in a way it never had been before. He told me that the words “Free Palestine” and the image of the Palestinian flag were hurtful to a lot of people he spoke with. I told him that if those words were more offensive than tens of thousands of Palestinian children being killed by Israel, then there was a fundamental disconnect between where those people stood and where I stood. But he couldn’t get past his public facing, “I don’t take sides.” And I get why people don’t. Taking a side can cost you. Money, brand deals, sponsorships, festivals, private shows, relationships and access. I’ve lost all of those things. But there is no neutral position between the oppressor and the oppressed. When one side has the bombs and bottomless financial and military support from America, refusing to take a side doesn’t leave you in the middle. What I said at MetLife I have been saying on stages around the world for almost three years. So why is it an issue now? Because now I’m sharing a stage with one of the biggest artists in the world, in some of the biggest stadiums in America. At a certain level of exposure, “Free Palestine” becomes too much of a risk. If I kept doing the shows, saying Free Palestine, with Ed implicitly supporting it, the crowd getting loud and showing undeniable support for Palestinian liberation, what artist might speak out next? The stage becomes resistance. Maybe that’s why this time it became so important to silence me. And one of the most effective ways to enforce that silence has been to weaponize the accusation of antisemitism. Antisemitism is real. And that is exactly why the word matters too much to be used as a shield against criticism of the Israeli state. When criticizing Israel, opposing Zionism or saying “Free Palestine” gets conflated with hatred of Jewish people, it doesn’t protect Jewish people. It protects Israel from accountability. I hope this isn’t the end of my relationship with Ed. Thirteen years of friendship doesn’t disappear because of one painful disagreement. I hope we both continue listening, studying what is happening in Palestine and wrestling with what neutrality means in a moment like this. My door will always be open to continuing that conversation. When my brother Omar was doing the subtitles for the video I posted from MetLife, I thanked him. He told me there’s a phrase in Arabic: “La shukra ala wajeb.” .لا شكر على واجب There is no thanks for a duty. That stayed with me. Because that’s what this has become for me and millions of others around the world. A duty. Not something deserving of praise or gratitude. Not brave. Human. Who is winning the internet, who is getting canceled, who gets to play the stadium and who doesn’t, all of it becomes so small when held against what we are actually witnessing in Gaza and the West Bank. An entire people being displaced, starved and killed while the world debates which words we are allowed to use to describe it, how those words make us feel, and whether our discomfort matters more than the people living through a genocide. I didn’t need 10 shows from Ed. I needed 2. Two chances to stand in front of 90,000 people and say the words that somehow became too dangerous to say. Free Palestine . But if those words cost me the stage, while turning the conversation back to Palestine, then it was the most successful tour I’ve ever been on.” The post Macklemore Controversy Creates an Uproar on Social Media appeared first on MLToday .

articles.title: Hakeem Jeffries, “Monkeys”, “Errand Boys”, and Black Misleadership
articles.author: MLToday
articles.content: By Margaret Kimberley, Black Agenda Report September 9, 2026 Hakeem Jeffries climbs the political ladder because he engages in dirty deeds with the world’s worst people. Being called a monkey gives him an easy out. The presence of a Black face in a high place is still rarely worth celebrating or defending. “He [Hakeem Jeffries] is a bought and paid AIPAC monkey. With all due respect, I don’t mean it in a racist way. He is basically just an errand boy.” – Rula Jebreal Should a racial slur be viewed differently if the target is a lackey for the oligarchs and therefore an enemy of Black people and indeed all of humanity? That is the question in the wake of Palestinian journalist Rula Jebreal’s unfortunate use of the word “monkey” to describe House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries while appearing on the Wahajat Ali podcast . Jebreal immediately realized that she had put her foot in her mouth and added the disclaimer at the end of her statement and the program host also made the same point , but the slur could not be unheard. Her description of Jeffries and nearly every other member of Congress as a Zionist tool was factually correct, but the ensuing controversy is instructive and illustrates the lingering power of the Black face in a high place. That dynamic creates a great deal of confusion that must be examined as a means of ending the retrograde politics that control this country. As readers know, this columnist stands firmly in the Black Agenda Report tradition of giving no quarter to Jeffries and other members of the group known as the Black misleadership class. They were described by Glen Ford thusly. “ ‘Black Misleadership class’ is not a ‘scientific’ term. It is weaponized political terminology, with specific meaning based on Black historical and current political realities. Most often, in our usage at Black Agenda Report, the term refers to those Black political forces that emerged at the end of the Sixties, eager to join the corporate and duopoly political (mostly Democrat) ranks, and to sell out the interests of the overwhelmingly working class Black masses in the process. It is both an actual and aspirational class, which ultimately sees its interests as tied to those of U.S. imperialism and its ruling circles. It seeks representation in the halls of corporate power, and dreads social transformation, which would upset the class’s carefully cultivated relationships with Power.” As the leader of the Democratic Party in the House of Representatives who may be the next Speaker of the House, Jeffries is surely in the category that Ford described. In my recent column, “ Hakeem Jeffries and Jared Kushner Meeting Reveals Ugly Truths About U.S. Politics ” I explained how much, or rather how little this position would mean for the betterment of Black people. “He would be the first Black Speaker, but to what end? Black people will be no better off with a scoundrel who happens to look like us. We have seen this movie, and we know how it ends, with nothing to show for the feeling of pride at seeing a Black face in a high place but one which has been vetted to ensure that Black people would benefit very little from their presence.” Jeffries’ meeting with Donald Trump’s son-in-law revealed what astute observers already know. The political system in this country is controlled by the ruling class for their benefit. Democrats may refer to Trump and his family as fascists engaged in corruption at the expense of the public and they are just that. Yet the leader of an alleged opposition party has back door meetings with those very same corrupt individuals because that is what the political system demands. Jeffries’ position is therefore inherently corrupt as well. He bows to Zionists like Kushner and to big pharma and insurance companies when he announces he does not support Medicare for All. Yet Jeffries was the recipient of adamant support and defense from millions of people because a slur was used against him. Black people being referred to as monkeys is deeply offensive, quite literally dehumanizing, and cannot be excused or explained away. Jebreal said as much and later offered an unqualified apology but the lure of protecting a prominent Black person and acknowledging the deeply felt emotions when Black people are in any way disparaged created a firestorm and also revealed the complexities of Black political interactions with other groups. Many of the Jeffries defenders were most angry that a Palestinian called him a monkey. “Arabs are racists.” “Palestinians put Trump in the White House.” “That’s why I don’t care about Gaza.” These and other missives could be seen and heard widely across all social media. The Afropessimists felt vindicated as they pointed to what they claimed was a universally held racist view among people who aren’t Black and the Foundational Black Americans (FBA) were pleased at having been proven correct about a subject they usually boast about having no position on or any interest in at all. No one in these groups is ever mobilized against genocide or imperialism nor do they have much to say about domestic issues such as mass incarceration, police violence, or gentrification and other methods of capitalist exploitation. Yet they emerged from self-imposed silence to denounce and condemn on a subject they happily ignored in the past. Many of Jebreal’s defenders were no better. Instead of making their case against Jeffries and the rest of the political class in their support of AIPAC and the Zionist state, they chose to delve into Black politics which they knew nothing about. It is somewhat interesting that Jeffries condemned Black conservatives like Clarence Thomas in 1992 when he was a university student, but a Black person making a political critique against another Black person and referring to them as a “house slave” is in no way comparable to the use of a racial slur by someone who isn’t Black. Jebreal’s supporters made a serious error when they chose that and other lines of defense. The mistake is not really surprising, given that the Democratic Party misleaders jumped on the chance to make themselves relevant with the Black people they usually ignore while also making their Zionist bosses happy. Like Afropessimists and those who call themselves FBA, the misleaders wasted no time in trying to score points.The Congressional Black Caucus , willing accomplices to AIPAC control, felt compelled to join in the attack on Jebreal. “We have to stop platforming and trafficking in anti-Black racism, whether it’s on the political right or the left.” Operatives like Symone Sanders-Townsend were also, as they say, up in their feelings. “Also…if Democrats win the House in November, I am very sure Hakeem Jeffries will become the Speaker. He will be third in line to the presidency. Respect will also be due then. Respect does not mean you agree with strategy or the decisions, but it does mean you should (at the very least) watch your tone.” The Speaker of the House is a public servant accountable to the public and not a member of royalty. No one needs to watch their tone if Jeffries wields the gavel in Congress. Also, the Speaker is in fact second in line to the presidency, but I digress from more important points. Ironically, Hakeem Jeffries himself is probably relieved about Jebreal’s statement. The Kushner meeting is now treated as some sort of ancient history, now forgotten in the heat of unscrupulous people feeling the need to jump into the fray and promote themselves to the gullible. As for the term “errand boy,” this columnist has done so many times in describing not only Jeffries, but the entire U.S. political class, such as in the Kushner meeting column. “Voters in this country rarely get what they want because the Kushners of the world call the shots with the help of their errand boys and girls, who are otherwise known as party leaders.” They are all errand boys and errand girls, and no one should hesitate to describe them as such. We live in a society that promotes empty suits like Jeffries, an ambitious but vacuous man who will support war crimes and apartheid in Palestine and deaths caused by a profit-motivated health care system in the U.S. I will not call Jeffries a monkey.The word snake may be more appropriate for Jeffries and all of his ilk if we’re sticking with an animal analogy. After all, Washington is a nest of vipers. Margaret Kimberley is the author of Prejudential: Black America and the Presidents . The post Hakeem Jeffries, “Monkeys”, “Errand Boys”, and Black Misleadership appeared first on MLToday .

articles.title: Portugal: Communists Celebrate Five Decades of Democracy and Struggle
articles.author: MLToday
articles.content: By Luke Rotello and Moth Wisnewski, People’s World September 11, 2026 Above photo: The crowd was tens-of-thousands’strong at the Avante! Festival in Seixal, Portugal this past weekend. Photo via Avante! Seixal, Portugal—Hundreds of thousands of Communists, workers, youth, and their allies joined the 50th anniversary of the Avante! Festival (Festa do Avante!) from Sept. 4 to 6 in Seixal, Portugal, a suburb just outside the capital, Lisbon. The event is named for Avante! , or Forward! in English, the newspaper of the Portuguese Communist Party, which organizes the massive gathering. Held annually, the festival celebrates Portugal’s struggle for democracy after the 1974 Carnation Revolution, a bloodless coup orchestrated by left- and Communist-aligned sections of the Portuguese military. It brought an end to the fascist Estado Novo regime, which ruled the country through terrorism and political repression for over 40 years. While imprisoning and torturing thousands of Communists domestically, the Estado Novo’s violence was most extensive in territories subject to Portuguese colonization. Powerful anti-colonial movements organized in Guinea-Bissau, Cabo Verde, Angola, Mozambique, Timor-Leste, and elsewhere in the Portuguese empire began waging struggles for independence in the 1960s. By the time of the revolution, the Estado Novo had murdered hundreds of thousands of people, mostly civilians. The Carnation Revolution, named for the carnations placed in soldiers’ guns as a symbol of peace, ended the colonial wars against liberation movements and brought a return to democracy—only this time with workers taking the lead. Through an unstable transitional period marked by strikes, mass agitation, and counter-revolutionary conspiracies, Portugal elected a constituent assembly with a substantial Communist presence that gave rise to the progressive 1976 Constitution, now celebrated every year at the festival. A celebration of progress The festival organizes and anchors a tremendous range of cultural events, with a program spanning literature, art galleries, theater, cinema, sciences, political debates, dance, and music. Small crowds formed around drum troops in thoroughfares while symphony orchestras and rock bands drew thousands, their performances punctuated by slogans such as “25 de abril sempre, fascismo nunca mais” (“April 25th forever; fascism never again”). Branches of the Communist Party in Lisbon operate large stalls with food, information, and merchandise, while the regional sections of the PCP outside of the city operate their own booths representing the economy and culture of the country’s districts. Regional staple foods are served next to artistic exhibits and murals bearing regional demands: for universal public transportation, against the privatization of national parks, and for food sovereignty, among others. As one member of the Juventude Comunista Portuguesa (JCP), the party’s youth league, explained, the presentation of food is also political, whether reflecting culinary traditions drawn from ethnic and religious repression or from the country’s ongoing struggle for food sovereignty. The European Union (EU) imposes economic measures that privilege production of specific goods by country, bringing the Portuguese agricultural sector (as well as its immense strides in land reform and collectivization) from a state of self-sufficiency into dependency on imported goods. As these costs have come down on the rural working class, Portugal’s largest cities and most popular tourist destinations have confronted housing speculation and informalization of the economy. The forced de-industrialization of the country has been paired with increases in freedom of movement for EU citizens, shifting the entire economy toward tourism and pushing wider sections of the working class out of their historic neighborhoods and into the hospitality industry and contingent labor. Political unity against the far-right Not all attendees are directly affiliated with the PCP, but the party’s message of popular defense of the civil freedoms enshrined in the constitution by the 1974 revolution draws crowds from many elements of left and progressive movements in the country. Plus, young people from all backgrounds flock in for the hit parade of music acts that fill the schedule every day and evening of the festival. Murals displaying pieces of the Portuguese constitution decorated stalls and walkways throughout the festival. Whether in the Young Pioneers area or the international section, the defense of legal rights of working people was the primary cultural current throughout. As the political right has taken up a legal struggle to erode or reinterpret elements of the constitution, the PCP reminds festival attendees that the fight for civil freedoms is a continual process that must grapple with new political and economic realities as they arise. One JCP member compared Article 73 of the constitution, which guarantees that scientific innovations will advance in the spirit of collective benefit and democracy, with the real difficulties transgender Portuguese citizens face in seeking gender-affirming care. They emphasized the dangers posed by sectarian forces tactically aligning with the far-right to challenge elements of the constitution while failing to defend the democratic rights it promises. The festival this year took place amidst the political ascendancy of Chega (Enough!), Portugal’s far-right and MAGA-esque party. Signs featuring Chega slogans promising a “clean” Portugal now blanket Lisbon, covering thousands of streetlight poles with the face of the party’s leader. Many years of alternating governance split between Portugal’s Socialist Party (PS) and Social Democratic Party (PSD) has left those parties stagnant and unable to mediate the relationships between labor and both small and large capital interests. Because of this, finance capital has been given more maneuverability—exerting influence both inside and outside the PS and PSD, and mediating a transition of power into the hands of the far-right. Despite this, the PCP has stood as a stalwart defender of the constitution, peace, and progress. This was on full display during this past year’s two general strikes in December and June, led by the General Confederation of Portuguese Workers (CGTP-IN) that defeated the government’s proposed labor package and awakened a new level of consciousness in the Portuguese people regarding the true intentions of the far-right. Palestinian solidarity was a major theme of the event, with representatives of the Palestine Liberation Organization tabling in the international delegate section, Palestinian artists performing in the music lineup, and Palestinian flags decorating many official displays or being flown by attendees. Internationalist to the core As the festival closed out on Sunday evening, tens of thousands of party members and attendees took up the flags of the PCP and JCP and filled the plaza in front of the main stage. Chants of “P-C-P!” and “Cuba vencerá!” [“Cuba will win!”] took the crowd by storm. Children and elders alike took their seats for speeches by PCP leaders, including General Secretary Paulo Raimundo, who reaffirmed the party’s support for the international movement in defense of Palestine, saying: “The solidarity lacking from governments bent to the U.S. and Israel, as exemplified by the [PS/PSD] government that stubbornly refuses to recognize the state of Palestine, comes to you from the people who take to the street worldwide—and Portugal is no exception!” The closing address also included a video presentation by Cuban President Miguel Díaz-Canel. Saluting the PCP for its struggle in defense of Cuba’s sovereignty, Díaz-Canel expressed the solidarity of the Communist Party of Cuba. “What the imperialists cannot forgive us for,” he said, “is the dignity, the courage, the ideological commitment, spirit of sacrifice, and revolutionary spirit of the Cuban people. Long live our Communist Parties!” By the end of the speeches, the crowd was electric with anticipation of the festival’s final moments: renditions of “The Internationale,” “Avante, Camarada!” and the “Carvalhesa,” anthem of the festival movement. Where international working-class unity had been the message in speech, it was brought to life again in dance with tens of thousands of comrades bearing Communist flags from all corners of the planet, and with carnations in hands and minds. The post Portugal: Communists Celebrate Five Decades of Democracy and Struggle appeared first on MLToday .

articles.title: NPR Blames Cuba for What the Blockade Did
articles.author: MLToday
articles.content: By Lea Aschkenas September 5, 2026 Resumen English Recently, while listening to an NPR (National Public Radio) interview with Cuban-American musician Arturo Sandoval, I was reminded of the late political scientist Michael Parenti’s classic text, Inventing Reality: The Politics of the Mass Media . In his 1986 book, Parenti described a situation that is still relevant forty years later— when the US fears that another country’s non-capitalistic political model (and its attendant advances in social justice and quality of life) could cause US citizens to question their own system, it regularly imposes an embargo and sanctions against the country. Next, the news media reports on the suffering caused by these policies while, at the same time, avoiding any mention of the embargo and sanctions. Finally, when after years or decades of suffering, the people of this blockaded country take out their anger on the closest target and begin protesting against their government, the US steps in. It places a puppet president in power and pours into the country the money it had withheld throughout the embargo. Then, the media reports on how well everyone is now doing without, once more, acknowledging the oversized role the embargo played in the prior devastation. In the aforementioned NPR interview, host Scott Simon perfectly perpetuated this model of media complicity by announcing towards the interview’s conclusion, “Arturo Sandoval, I’ve got to put you on the spot a little. You’ve been pretty quiet about politics over the years, but obviously you, you [sic] fled Cuba. When Fidel Castro died, you spoke out about your disdain for his regime. It was ten years ago.” Then, with no historical or even recent context, Simon concluded with, “Cuba seems to be almost worse than ever now.” With this final declaration in which he erroneously implied a connection between Cuba’s current immiseration and Fidel Castro’s rule, Simon led Sandoval into his response: “Sixty-seven years and a half is way too long, man… The people in Cuba are desperate and hopeless.” Simon allowed his guest to say this unchallenged as if these decades of desperation and hopelessness are the result of Cuba’s 1959 revolution. To the contrary, in addition to footing the bill for Sandoval’s musical education (he attended the free Cuban National Art School, founded by Fidel Castro), the Cuban Revolution redefined human rights as access for all to free education, free healthcare, low-cost daycare centers, and highly-subsidized housing. The desperation Sandoval referred to is the direct result of the US’s 67-year-old embargo against Cuba, the longest embargo in the history of the world. Combined with its multitude of supplementary sanctions (more than 200 of which were enacted during Trump’s first term in office), these punitive measures prohibit Cuba from purchasing products, including medicine, manufactured abroad if they contain more than 10% of US-origin components. They restrict US residents’ ability to travel to Cuba. They hinder Cubans residing in the US from wiring money to their families, a common way for immigrants from all parts of the world to supplement the income of relatives back home. The Cuban embargo has received worldwide condemnation. For more than three decades now, the UN General Assembly has annually presented its members with a resolution to denounce the embargo. Year after year, its 193 member states cast a near unanimous vote affirming the resolution. The only two countries who consistently vote against it— and in favor of the embargo— are, unsurprisingly, the US and Israel. Unfortunately, the UN resolution, while a significant show of solidarity, has no authority to end the embargo. As codified by US law, only the US Congress has this power. Sadly, also, the suffering caused by the embargo is not a mere result of it but the explicit objective of it as stated in a declassified 1960 government document posted on the National Security Archive’s website and abstracted as follows: “This memo, written by Deputy Assistant Secretary of State for Inter-American Affairs Lestor Mallory, provides the original, unvarnished, policy rationale for imposing trade restrictions on Cuba. Fidel Castro’s revolution is quite popular in Cuba, Mallory points out; since there is no effective opposition against him, the only way to undercut Castro’s support is ‘through disenchantment and disaffection based on economic dissatisfaction and hardship.’ Mallory advocates a set of punitive economic actions designed to deny ‘money and supplies to Cuba, to decrease monetary and real wages, to bring about hunger, desperation, and the overthrow of [the] government.’” Beyond the embargo and its sanctions, the US’s designation of Cuba as a State Sponsor of Terrorism (SSOT) contributes to what Sandoval referred to as the Cuban people’s hopelessness and desperation. The partisan political boomerang of the SSOT was initiated by Ronald Reagan in 1982 for Cuba’s support of Latin American leftist groups. It was removed by Obama in 2015, reinstated by Trump in 2021, symbolically removed by Biden on January 14 th , 2025 at the end of his presidency, and again reinstated by Trump on January 20 th , 2025 at the start of his second term. Along with other restrictions, the sponsor-of-terrorism status forbids US international aid organizations, including Food for Peace and the Peace Corps, from offering humanitarian assistance to Cuba. It prohibits Cuba from receiving loans from the World Bank and other international financial institutions. These are loans which could be used for much-needed projects such as an overhaul of the island’s aging electrical grid, which has caused multiple nationwide blackouts over the past two years. Furthermore, as described by the Washington Office on Latin America, the SSOT “has a chilling effect on businesses, including banking or telecommunications investments that are crucial to promoting the type of transformation essential to expanding freedom on the island.” Ironically, this freedom (ie: the opening of business and economic opportunities) is precisely what the US purports to desire for the Cuban people. And it is this lack of this freedom, which Sandoval said in the somber closing statement of his NPR interview, that prevents him from returning to Cuba and will leave him to “die dreaming” of a homecoming. At this point in the interview, what Scott Simon didn’t say becomes as, if not more, significant than what he did. It is that, in Fidel Castro’s final two years of life, a sense of hope and a feeling of, yes, freedom pervaded Cuba. Hope came to Cubans with Obama’s 2014 détente, which, while not a revocation of the embargo, still enabled the US Embassy in Cuba and the Cuban Embassy in the US to reopen for the first time in 50 years. Washington’s rapprochement permitted commercial and direct mail flights between the two countries to be reinstated and for restrictions on remittances to be loosened. This, in turn, allowed Cuban-Americans, like immigrants from other countries, to now easily send money to their families on the island. Freedom came from an opening of the Cuban economy, from the government’s expanded opportunities for private businesses. Cubans responded enthusiastically, opening record numbers of cafés and restaurants and music and art venues, among other enterprises to which their new American friends, now able to travel freely to Cuba, flocked in record numbers. It was a boon for both sides— and evidence that another way of engaging with Cuba was possible. Until, that is, Trump was elected at the end of 2016 and, soon thereafter, began systematically shutting everything down once more. If not for the very real damage it inflicts on the country, the SSOT designation could be considered laughable as, during all these decades as a supposed sponsor of terrorism, Cuba has remained steadfast in its commitment to a peaceful coexistence with its neighbors near and far. For the past quarter of a century, Cuba’s Latin American Medical School, esteemed for both its size (enrollment-wise, it is considered the largest medical school in the world) and its focus on preventative healthcare, has offered a full-ride, plus a monthly living stipend, for students from low-income communities around the world, including the US. Additionally, in the wake of Hurricane Katrina, Cuba offered aid workers to the US, although President Bush rebuffed this overture. In the early days of COVID-19, Cuba sent medical brigades to help Italy contain its outbreak. And this was in addition to the doctors Cuba regularly sent to countries in need from Algeria to Honduras to Sri Lanka. Until, that is, in 2025 the US began threatening to deny visas to the leaders of countries accepting assistance from Cuban doctors; and the targeted countries, fearing retribution, terminated their contracts with Cuba. This past March, as Jamaica’s Cuban doctors headed home following one such termination, hundreds of Jamaicans took the streets for what they called a “Gratitude Walk.” For three miles, they marched wearing t-shirts reading, “Thank you Cuba for 50 years of medical service” and chanting, “We love Cuba” and “Bring back the doctors.” Walk participant Rupert Walters, President of the Jamaica-Cuba Friendship Association’s St. Catherine’s chapter and a beneficiary of Cuban care for his prostate cancer, called his government’s decision to cave to US pressure “crazy.” Walters told the Jamaica Observer that he wished the government had “allowed the Cubans to support and give their services to the hundreds of thousands of Jamaicans who can’t afford it,” and warned that, as a result of the medical program termination, Jamaicans would die. Rather than supporting terrorism, Cuba has long been the target of terrorist attacks by the US government. There were the CIA’s half-century of documented assassination attempts against Fidel Castro, involving everything from poison pens to exploding cigars. Less comical and more lethal were terrorist attacks led by Luis Posada Carriles, a Cuban exile and CIA-operative. In 1976, thirty-five years before September 11 th , Posada Carriles masterminded the Western Hemisphere’s first act of political terrorism against a civilian flight. His bombing of a Cubana de Aviación airplane killed all 73 passengers, 24 of whom comprised the entirety of the Juvenile Cuban National Fencing team. In the summer of 1997, Posada Carrilles began another bombing campaign, this time targeting Havana hotels, restaurants, and discotheques— and killing an Italian tourist. Finally arrested in Panama in 2000 for attempting to assassinate Fidel Castro at a conference he was attending there, Posada Carrilles later fled to the US where he was detained for illegal entry and then pardoned by President Bush. In 2018, he died a free man in Miami. Although Scott Simon didn’t say this in his interview with Arturo Sandoval, the current “worse-than-ever” situation he referenced is due to the US’s oil blockade, initiated by an Executive Order from Trump in January. Under this latest act of economic warfare, tankers trying to deliver petroleum to the island are threatened with tariffs and, if they still attempt to do so, they are chased away by US Coast Guard vessels. Like the embargo, like the sanctions, like the SSOT status, the fuel blockade has caused widespread suffering for the Cuban people. It impedes access to electricity and also to water, which arrives at most houses in Cuba via an electric pump. It prevents the preservation of not just food but also of medicines that need refrigeration. Many Cubans now sleep outside, on rooftops or on the Malecón seawall, to escape the sweltering summer heat, made all the more unbearable without the electricity to run their fans. Because electricity (which has been prioritized for hospitals and schools) is now available in most houses for just two hours per day, Cubans must wake up whenever it arrives (even if it is at 3 AM) to do all they couldn’t without it— wash clothes and dishes, cook and bathe. And collect water for the next outage. So, sleep too, has become a casualty of this US-provoked humanitarian crisis, referred to by a group of US Representatives who visited the island in July as a “silent Gaza.” By engaging in de-contextualized reporting rather than shedding light on the reasons why the current situation is as it is, mainstream US media outlets like NPR do their listeners a grave and dangerous disservice. For, as The Washington Post ’s motto warns us, albeit a little more ironically after Jeff Bezos’ purchase of it, “Democracy dies in darkness.” Citizens who are not given the context of the news cannot be engaged participants in the democratic process. Without the full story as to why what is happening in our world is happening, we are rendered powerless to change it. Without our consent, we become cogs in the bulldozer of US interventionism and imperialism. Life in Cuba is full of suffering not because of socialism but because of a 67-year-long blockade by the world’s largest superpower. In a government now absent of checks and balances, we need to call out the offending media. We need to let them know that we’re paying attention, that we hold them accountable for their lies of omission— and that we demand better. Lea Aschkenas is the author of the memoir, Es Cuba: Life and Love on an Illegal Island (Seal Press/Hachette) and the children’s book, Arletis, Abuelo, and the Message in a Bottle (Star Bright Books). She lived in Cuba in the year 2000 and has returned regularly ever since. She lives in Northern California where she works as a public librarian and a poet-teacher with the California Poets in the Schools program. articles.title: The Struggle against Industrial Expansion in Cancer Alley
articles.author: MLToday
articles.content: By Kennith RaShaun Woods II, Inequality.org Communities in Louisiana are fighting, including against their own governments, to block new polluting projects. Residents of Cancer Alley are deeply familiar with disease and death. Many of them, especially the region’s Black communities, have witnessed their loved ones suffer from asthma, diabetes and cancer. They have watched them die. Sprawling chemical plants spewing waste into the air sit just down the street. The smell of toxins never quite goes away. This region is the 85-mile corridor between Baton Rouge and New Orleans, Louisiana. This stretch of southern Louisiana contains nine parishes that sit along the Mississippi River. There are around 200 gas and chemical plants in Cancer Alley, and most of these plants were built on or near former plantations. “[There is] one street where 80 percent of the people on the street are either living with cancer or they have a family member who has passed away from cancer. It’s been depressing…there’s communities that are boxed in. They have industry on both sides of their communities,” Shamell Lavigne told Inequality.org in an interview. She is the chief operating officer for RISE St. James , an environmental advocacy group in St. James Parish. The risk of cancer in the corridor is the highest in the nation. Several studies confirm what Black residents on the ground have been feeling for decades: their bodies are being sacrificed for industrial development and capital accumulation. For example, a 2023 study found that “reported emissions of common industrial pollutants” are seven to 21 times higher in communities of color than in white communities. ProPublica mapped out “sacrifice zones” across the U.S., which are populated areas with high levels of pollution coming from industrial production. The Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) “threshold for an acceptable level of cancer risk,” at least in 2023, was 1 in 10,000. This means the presence of carcinogens from chemical plants would lead to one more person developing cancer out of 10,000 across their lifetime. There are several sacrifice zones in Louisiana. Shell, in particular, controls many plants along the Mississippi River with emissions above the EPA level. The Shell Convent refinery just outside Sorrento is 2.1 times over the accepted risk level; the Shell plant in Norco, Louisiana, is 8.5 times over the accepted risk level; and the Shell plant in Geismar is 16 times the EPA’s acceptable risk. Community members across Cancer Alley’s nine parishes have formed advocacy groups to mount legal challenges against chemical companies and the corrupt local parish councils who continue to greenlight industrial development, despite the well-known health risks. RISE St. James was founded in 2018 by Sharon Lavigne to combat Formosa Plastics’ attempt to build a massive chemical plant in St. James Parish’s majority-Black 5th District. That legal fight against the proposed plant, entitled the “Sunshine Project,” is still ongoing, and has thus far been arduous but successful. Formosa Plastics has yet to build the plant. However, it has received a fourth preconstruction permit from the Louisiana Department of Environmental Quality, even though Formosa Plastics is unable to meet revised safety standards. “We’re going up against $1 billion companies with limited resources, so it can be pretty difficult. We rely on our faith that things will be better, and if we keep fighting, we can stop some of these polluters from killing us,” Lavigne said. The environmental advocacy group has since expanded its operations to help other local groups fight against industrial expansion in neighboring parishes, including Ascension and St. John the Baptist. One of their many ongoing battles is against the St. James Parish council itself. RISE St. James, alongside Inclusive Louisiana and Mount Triumph Baptist Church, has accused St. James Parish of violating Black residents’ rights and constitutional protections through greenlighting petrochemical development and rezoning majority-Black areas for industrial use. The Center for Constitutional Rights and the Tulane Environmental Law Clinic are providing legal support to the plaintiffs. They are seeking a moratorium on new petrochemical construction projects, with the ultimate goal of freeing the parish’s economy from petrochemical companies. That coalition initially filed its lawsuit in March 2023, kickstarting a yearslong legal slugfest with St. James Parish, which filed a motion to dismiss the lawsuit in June 2023. The Eastern District of Louisiana, a U.S. federal district court, dismissed many of the plaintiff’s claims in November 2023. The setback did not deter the local advocacy groups; instead, they filed an appeal in the U.S Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals, and in April 2025, the court ruled the case could move forward . It was a monumental win, and it kept the fight against environmental racism in St. James Parish alive. Once again, St. James Parish filed to dismiss the lawsuit in November 2025, bringing the case back to the Eastern District of Louisiana. That set up a hearing on Jan. 28 in New Orleans and a decision on Feb. 9. The federal case against St. James Parish The plaintiffs allege St. James Parish has violated several constitutional, federal and state rights through their land use patterns in majority-Black areas. Among them are alleged violations of the Thirteenth Amendment, the Fourteenth Amendment, the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act and the right to historical and cultural preservation in the Louisiana Constitution. The Thirteenth Amendment abolished slavery outside of prison. Subsequent cases affirmed Congress’ “power to pass all laws necessary and proper for abolishing all badges and incidents of slavery in the United States.” RISE St. James, Inclusive Louisiana and Mt. Triumph Baptist Church allege St. James Parish conjured the “badges and incidents,” or the historical consequences, of slavery through their discriminatory pattern of land use. They cite a 2014 land use plan, which has since been amended, that redesignated majority-Black areas in the parish as “industrial” or “residential/future industrial.” Additionally, since the first plant was constructed in the parish in 1958, at least 28 out of 32 plants have been built in the majority-Black 4th and 5th districts. These plants are often built directly on former plantations. The “badges and incidents of slavery” in this case are clear: several thousand acres of plantation land once used for slavery is now being used to house sprawling chemical plants that dilute Black communities with carcinogens. The plaintiffs also allege St. James Parish violated the Fourteenth Amendment’s Equal Protection Clause through their land use pattern. Alongside the disproportionate buildout of chemical plants in majority-Black areas, they cite how the 2014 land use plan was adopted to prevent Wolverine Terminals Corporation and Petroplex International from building oil storage facilities in majority-white areas. The plan also concentrated most two-mile buffer zones in majority-white areas in the parish. Majority-white churches and schools were afforded some level of protection from exposure to chemical pollution; majority-Black institutions were not provided such mercy. Finally, the advocacy groups allege that industrial development on burial sites of the formerly enslaved violates their state constitutional “right of the people to preserve, foster, and promote their respective historic linguistic and cultural origins” and the 1993 Religious Land Use and Individualized Persons Act. The Code Noir, a set of laws governing the practice of slavery during French and Spanish rule in the 17th and 18th centuries, required slave owners to bury enslaved people on consecrated ground. “Enslaved people were generally buried on uncultivated land in the back of the plantation, further away from the Mississippi River and in or at the edge of the forest…By the time of Emancipation there were likely several cemeteries of enslaved people within each plantation,” the initial 2023 moratorium complaint said. These were typically unmarked graves, and plantation owners seldom recorded enslaved people’s deaths. Loved ones planted trees to mark burial sites, but beyond that, identifying enslaved people, finding burial sites and tracing family lineages is tragically cumbersome. Forensic Architecture identified potential unmarked cemeteries across several former plantations that now house petrochemical plants. According to them, this means “hundreds, if not thousands, of cemeteries [are] at risk from industrial activity.” Indeed, plants including the Rain CII calcined coke plant and the Mosaic Faustina fertilizer plant have desecrated unmarked cemeteries in the parish, according to the complaint. RISE St. James, Inclusive Louisiana and Mount Triumph Baptist Church lay out an argument of explicit racial and ecological discrimination against St. James Parish due to its patterns of land use. Their greenlighting of petrochemical projects in majority-Black areas and treatment of the formerly enslaved tie directly to historical vestiges of slavery. Black residents are burdened by chemicals and high cancer risk, they cannot pray over their deceased ancestors and their ancestors themselves cannot rest in peace. Their arguments thoroughly convinced the Eastern District of Louisiana. In February, the federal district court allowed each claim to proceed, stating that St. James Parish’s land use pattern “quite literally originated in slavery.” “How many of us have to die? This ruling affirms what we know in our hearts and our faith: God did not create our communities to be sacrificed,” Lavigne from RISE St. James said. State and local government collaboration with industry The fight against St. James Parish is now in the discovery phase. Though the parish lost mightily to its own residents, it still continues to support industrial development. On June 17, the council voted to redesignate the majority-Black town Romeville from “agricultural” to “industrial,” opening the door for even more development in Black communities. RISE St. James, Inclusive Louisiana and Mount Triumph Baptist Church filed a motion for a temporary restraining order the following day. “We feel left out, because every time we go to the council meeting or the planning commission, it seems like their minds have already been made up [to be] pro-industry,” said Inclusive Louisiana co-founder Barbara Washington. St. James Parish’s behavior is typical of local and state governments desperate for industry money. The Louisiana Department of Environmental Quality’s excessive permit granting to polluters, non-disclosure agreements between Ascension Parish officials and Hyundai Steel and a non-disclosure agreement between Meta and Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry himself are all examples of local and state officials selling Louisianians out to any massive company who wants to set up shop in the state. These officials parrot lies about high-paying jobs and economic prosperity, which has yet to come to Cancer Alley’s Black communities. In fact, Black residents are underrepresented in the highest-paying chemical manufacturing jobs and overrepresented in the lowest-paying jobs in the industry. Louisiana leaders are responsible for creating and expanding Cancer Alley. “It’s just sad. It’s sad that the politicians are putting profit over people,” Lavigne said. The sheer will and love for community expressed by local advocacy groups is an inspiring thing to witness. RISE St. James, Inclusive Louisiana and Mount Triumph Baptist Church have all brushed up against the overwhelming forces of the parish, the state and the judicial system multiple times over, and refuse to back down from environmental racism. Their concerted efforts, though, reveal an ugly truth. The parish and the state, these machines of oppressive power, are invested in the degradation of Black life. Several studies on Cancer Alley reaffirm the monstrous health risks for the corridor’s disproportionately Black residents. The facts are inarguable. These residents continue to voice their opposition to petrochemical development in council meetings, through environmental and racial organizing and through the legal system. Still, the parishes and the state persist. Louisiana must house more chemical plants, it must allow companies to pollute our bodies with toxic waste. It must sacrifice Black lives, and the beautiful, culturally rich landscapes along the Mississippi River, at the altar of maximum capital accumulation. This is nothing new. As the Eastern District put it, this is a pattern of suffering originated in slavery. Regardless of the mode of production or its exports, regardless if the industry is dominated by bondage or rife with carcinogens, the capital class accumulate wealth by harvesting Black anguish. In this region, Black bodies must be condemned to death, one way or another. Get involved While the plaintiffs prepare for the next court hearing, these advocacy groups are organizing residents and supporters against the parish council and chemical companies. Head to RISE St. James’ social media and website for ways to get involved, such as donating, attending council meetings, signing petitions or attending community meetings. The three-headed monster of white supremacy, capitalism and environmental degradation is alive and well in south Louisiana. Its strategy is different from the days of slavery, but terror it inflicts on Black communities remains the same. RISE St. James, among many other local advocacy groups, is fighting against this suffering, and scoring victories along the way. “It’s a lot of legal fights,” Lavigne said. “It’s been so much I can’t keep up with them all. But, it’s necessary to stop these polluters from poisoning us.” This struggle reminds us that life does not have to be like this in Cancer Alley. There doesn’t need to be a Cancer Alley at all. Industrial development is not inevitable, and neither is Black suffering. These organizations are paving a path toward a future free from chemical plants and the sight of loved ones succumbing to disease. In this future, the economy is equitable and people’s needs are sufficiently addressed. In this future, our ancestors finally get to rest in peace. Advocacy groups like RISE St. James are leading the way, and it is imperative that local residents in St. James Parish, and all throughout Cancer Alley, follow their lead.
